The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta raised a point of order about the allocation of time to speakers on report stage motions, it being within the Standing Orders that the mover of a motion is entitled to 40 minutes. Since there are groupings of motions which in fact reduced the possibility of speeches on separate motions, the difficulty which remains is this: should the mover of a motion which has been filed in time be deprived of his right to make a 40 minute speech within the standing orders just because it has been grouped with other motions?
I would be pleased to listen to contrary views but I must say I cannot see how the Chair can deprive the mover of a motion of his right to make a 40 minute speech simply because motions have been grouped for the purposes of discussions and voting. I think it would be an unfair extension of the rule to say that the mover should be deprived of his 40 minutes because his motion has been grouped in that way. Further, it would be extremely difficult for the Chair to decide which motion had been moved first, or which mover should, so to speak, have priority.
Thus it would seem fair to say that any mover of a motion, whether it be debated alone or in common with others, ought to be entitled to all that is coming to him, at least in terms of time allocation under the Standing Order, although I am sure it is not the hope of all that maximum advantage will be taken of that opportunity by every speaker.

Well, Mr. Speaker, the minister is using legal terms in talking about the difference between piracy and hijacking. The point I am making is that if somebody took a ship by means of piracy, it is the same sort of thing as hijacking. Under the present law, if the person who takes the ship by piracy kills somebody or attempts to kill somebody, he is going to pay the supreme penalty. Under the law that the Solicitor General is putting forward, if he kills everybody on the ship he is going to pay the same penalty as if he is caught and just walks off the ship. I think that kind of law is dangerous and it is why I think this section should be changed.
We have been talking about deterrence, and many times during the committee hearings the Solicitor General tried to show that Professor Isaac Ehrlich's studies on economics were not relevant. He quoted other people in committee who had said that everything that Professor Ehrlich had said was not relevant. I came across an article written by Michael T. Malloy headline "Punishment is a deterrent to crime; so say economists whose data seemingly refute reform the criminal theories".
What I think we should be arguing here is whether this provision of the bill constitutes a deterrent. It is a very important part of the bill. I should like to put some of this article on record because it contradicts some of the points made by the Solicitor General in committee. Mr. Malloy also refers to some very well known economists who support Dr. Ehrlich's theories. Mr. Malloy says:
July 6, 1976

One of the reasons we stoppped hanging, gassing, and electrocuting murderers in the United States was that the experts said it did no good. In study after study, they found no connection between a state's use of capital punishment and the rate at which its citizens were murdererd. The death penalty had already fallen into disuse when the Supreme Court struck down most capital punishment laws as unconstitutional in 1972.
As we know, Mr. Speaker, this decision was reversed a short while ago. He continues:
Even though the deterrent effect of the death penalty was not a major issue in that ruling, at least five of the nine justices took note of the scholarly evidence in their written opinions. The best studies, wrote Justice Thurgood Marshall, "demonstrate that there is no correlation between the murder rate and the presence or absence of the capital sanction."
Now a new breed of experts has come along with studies that challenge this and other beliefs about crime and punishment. If their findings become accepted by judges, politicians, and voters, they could shift the emphasis of our legal system from trying to reform criminals to deliberately punishing them.
Prof. Isaac Ehrlich of the University of Chicago has challenged the conventional wisdom about capital punishment. Using the economists' arcane techniques of econometrics, he seems to have demonstrated that the death penalty does work: His analysis suggests that seven or eight innocent lives are saved with every execution.
Ehrlich's analysis could affect the fates of hundreds of death-row prisoners, because the Supreme Court is expected to rule this year on whether all capital-punishment laws are unconstitutional.
As I mentioned earlier, the Supreme Court has made that ruling and has held that they are constitutional under certain conditions.
The article continues:
His study was so striking that even before it was published last year, the Justice Department submitted a typescript copy to the Court along with its brief in favour of the death penalty.
That is the point I think we should talk about. The United States Justice Department is in favour of capital punishment because the studies have shown there is a deterrent effect. I think in this clause especially we should be talking about deterrence.
To continue:
Erhlich's work on the death penalty may be ignored by the Court or discredited by other scholars. But other yound economists are bringing their computers and equations to the study of robbery, burglary, and crime in general. Poaching in a field that was long dominated by psychologists and sociologists, they approach it from a substantially different point of view.
"The standard criminologist has been living in a dream world for at least 150 years," says Prof. Gordon Tullock of Virginia Polytechnic Institute. "They've thought that the cause of crime is not the economic return sought by some people, but an illness or some sort of disease. Eighty per cent of the people who seriously think about crime think about punishment as a deterrent-except for the sociologists, and they wrote all the books."
Some of the books state flatly that punishment does not deter crime. More say there is no evidence that it does. This belief has changed the official mission of the criminal-justice system. Parole, probation, and the wideshpread use of indeterminate sentences (0 to 20 years for the same kind of crime) are largely based on the goal of reform rather than punishment. Even prisons are officially defined as "correctional" institutions and "reformatories."
"Economists tend to believe that crime, far from being the result of sickness or mental disorder, in most cases is simply a business-oriented economic activity which is undertaken for much the same reasons as other types of economic activity," Tullock and David Meiselman wrote in the preface to The Economics of Crime and Punishment.

"To reduce the frequency of crime, economists generally recommend we raise the costs of crime. It would be difficult to find a more revolutionary departure from the conventional wisdom."
"We postulate that people only decide to enter crime if they expect it to pay," says Prof. Gary S. Becker of the University of Chicago, who helped pioneer the application of econometrics to crime in the late '60s. "Whether, in fact, it does pay is more difficult to get numbers on; there have been studies indicating it does pay.
"Much of my work has been on the question of deterrence. I think we have reasonably strong evidence that people are deterred from crime (by the prospect of punishment). It is not committed only by sick persons who can't help it. The assertion has been made until now that criminals are not deterred. What evidence there is goes the other way."
"When imprisonment is more certain and more severe, those states that have more punishment tend to have less crime," says Alfred Blumstein of Carnegie-Mellon University, who heads a National Academy of Sciences panel that is examining all the evidence on deterrence. "That's what the statistics show. That's what everyone finds."
Blumstein is not convinced, however, that the connection that economists find between crime and punishment proves that punishment deters crime. He says the same figures could just as well show that crime deters punishment because out-of-hand crime rates overwhelm police and courts and prisons, making criminals less likely to be caught, convicted, or jailed.
There's a more obvious reason to challenge the economists. Remember that they start by assuming that people don't commit crimes unless the benefits outweigh the costs, and that therefore punishment should deter crime. Isn't it questionable when their econometric answers confirm their assumptions?
No, they reply, that's the way econometrics works. The practitioner starts with a set of assumptions, turns them into equations, and assembles the equations into a mathematical model. If his model works when it is fed known data from the past, then it is probably a fair approximation of the real world. If it doesn't, he goes back to the drawing board. Erhlich's model was fed murder and execution data from 1933 through 1967, and it seemed to work best when its equations were consistent with an estimate that one death sentence deterred seven or eight murders.
Mr. Erhlich's work has been backed up by some very strong professionals in this field. The Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) has presented arguments before the committee which I do not think have convinced many of us, yet the people who back up Dr. Erhlich's work are well respected in the fields of both economics and crime.
I suggest that in respect of this clause of the bill dealing with piracy we must think about deterring. I think there can be a deterrent in this area when you are thinking of a man who has pirated a ship and is holding hostages. If the penalty is the same as if he had murdered a few people this leaves those hostages in very great difficulty. Perhaps the individual might think that if he gets rid of all the evidence he would have a much better chance of getting away. I hope those listening to this debate will think about this very seriously. This clause is another very much like clause 2 which members of this House, even abolitionists, should consider very seriously supporting in order to protect those people who may be caught in this very serious situation.

Mr. Speaker, we can see the trick used by the minister probably to minimize the impact of his amendment. He completely puts aside what was essential in the previous bill, namely the condition that someone kills while attempting to commit piracy. The minister uses only the first part of the present bill, with which we all agree, to remove the part that is now controversial. It reminds me of the second reading vote which he regarded as an acceptance of his bill.
Mr. Speaker, there is a limit to talking nonsense. Everyone knows full well that the vote was merely intended to refer Bill C-84 to the standing committee of the House for detailed study, and mainly to call in witnesses. Indeed, it often happens that hon. members vote for a bill on second reading to refer it to committee and, when they are not satisfied with that study, those same hon. members vote against the bill on third reading.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we are simply disgusted with the government's refusal to call in Witnesses before the committee. We had intended to call in many witnesses but the minister simply refused to have it that way. He told us we had no need of that. That is why we brought in 14 amendments which you accepted, Mr. Speaker. All those amendments are intended to allow us to do in this House what we were unable to do in committee, because of the dictatorship of this government.
Mr. Speaker, I feel this must open the eyes of the population. Indeed the people are very much awake, and we now know that 90 per cent of them are against the action of the minister, are in fact in favour of keeping the death penalty.
Needless to say, I support the amendment on piracy.
A while ago I heard the Solicitor General call one of my colleagues back to order again with regard to the subject of piracy, saying that he was merely referring to the pirates of old, the old sea pirates. I think it might be wise to ask ourselves what piracy is today. Today, we are no longer living as people did 2,000 ago. In days of yore, a pirate was defined as an adventurer who combed the seas in search of brigandage. But with the years, we have come to call a pirate any man who grows rich through plunder. That is the modern definition of a pirate. Today, he may be a banker and nowadays in our sophisticated and mechanised society the most dangerous pirates do not operate either on the sea or on land but in the air. They are what we

normally and logically call air pirates and I was about to include among them all public transportation pirates who use the powerful weapon of human hostages to reach their goals. The reasons for all that piracy are many but I shall mention only the main ones. First of all the lust for money which involves sacrificing even human lives to get millions. Second, the release of some prisoners who are friends of the pirates, third piracy for national and ideological issues. Piracy may also be used to upset governments. To try to upset the government to protest against the establishment is also a kind of piracy which endangers human life and may even require murder.
Right now, we are going through a period of high crime rate and over the last 15 years we have witnessed all possible crimes in modern piracy. Scarcely one week elapses without the newspapers reporting a plane hold up by well armed and well trained terrorists, hostages taking a high official being kidnapped to fulfill political ends, and so forth. And what about kidnappings as they happened in the last few years, even in our small regions where sordid murders took place, following seclusions to get a few thousands dollars? I still remember the sad autumn in Quebec when minister Laporte was executed by a gang of terrorists, after being kidnapped and secluded for a long time. Even buses filled with schoolboys were used as hostages by bandits to get to their ends.
We see so many kidnappings and crimes increasing at the same pace as the law is flouted because responsible people became irresponsible, wishing to abolish the only punishment that might clean up our society from all these crooks, who are multiplying every time they win a battle over law and order forces. As far as I am concerned, I say that pirates are winners when they manage to get everything they want from some country's authorities and even having themselves flown into a country of their own choice at public expense after disturbing peace and often committing the worst assassinations.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder when the government, instead of acting hypocritically as it does today, will wake up and come to support police forces and all prison guards who are clamouring for government action, for more rigid legislation, first to be protected and then to protect the entire population. Far from doing this, we are letting everything go. One of these days we are going to wake up in the most complete anarchy. The present minister will probably not be here any more. He will have run away, but the people will face the consequences of his action today. In the face of all this, the minister has nothing better to do than proposing life imprisonment for misfits in clause 3 of his bill C-84. But what does life imprisonment mean to the minister? This is a question we have to ask ourselves now because we cannot trust what he says. We judge man according to his actions because he must indeed be judged so. Past actions stand as evidence of things to come and the past is not good at all. Here is the evidence for this. Over the years, although he had promised to impose capital punishment on all those who would kill police officers and prison guards, what has he done? Nothing at all, Mr. Speaker. Since then, many police officers have been killed by the bandits they were trying to arrest, and never did the present minister have the courage to live up to the promise he had made here in the House. Are we doing to trust him again when he suggests life imprisonment for acts of

piracy? In my opinion, when the minister says "life imprisonment", he may mean, depending on his whim, 25 years, or 10 years, or even 5 years.
The Solicitor General should cease making meaningless promises which he never keeps. For, if this clause is not eliminated, air pirates-and God knows we hear of many of them every day, people who take over airplanes and keep hundreds of passengers as hostages-will continue to multiply, because they will know they can count on the laws of this country to protect them. Society is so insecure today that a great many people dare not travel by plane, for fear of meeting a new group of bandits. And yet, everybody rejoice when military authorities carry out some daring action, such as the successful one by the Israeli forces, even at the possible cost of innocent lives. Let us suppose for a moment that these pirates had succeeded in their blackmail attempt, the main purpose of which was to obtain the liberation of their partners held behind bars; there would now be eight more heroes among these air pirates. And the fear among the public would be eight times greater, and so would be the fear within the country. After all this killing, these acts of piracy, the minister cannot help crying over the fate of the killers, but what has he done and what is he doing for the victims of these hired killers? Nothing, less than nothing.
They do not even mention their names. Whereas those victims will be handicapped for the rest of their lives, our noble murderers will have an easy time in other countries or comfortably accommodated in our detention centres at the expense of all Canadian workers. Some will wait for parole which the minister, as ever, will grant them generously, while others will watch for an escape opportunity to get out and commit other heinous crimes or even murders since they do not have anything to fear any more in this respect.
I have always held the principle that the most efficient way to clear out weeds is to get rid of them. It is the same for society, Mr. Speaker. I am not wondering whether capital punishment is a means or the best deterrent to prevent other crimes. I say that the best way to prevent other crimes is to do away with criminals. Contrary to life imprisonment, capital punishment prevents any escape and all law abiding citizens can live peacefully.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the two motions now before us which deal with the matter of piracy which is now found in sections 75 and 76 of the Criminal Code. First, I should like to challenge the comment of the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) that somehow or other skyjacking is not piracy under the existing law. I find that very surprising and I think it is another example of the Solicitor General perhaps not even understanding the Criminal Code which he has been called upon to administer.
The motion that we have before us proposes that clause 3 of Bill C-84 be deleted. Clause 3 simply refers to subsection (2) of section 75 of the Criminal Code. To make this debate relevant I think it is necessary, first of all, to look at subsection (1) of section 75. Subsection (1) states: "Everyone commits piracy who does any act that by the laws of
Capital Punishment
nations is piracy". In short, what we must do to define piracy-whether or not the Solicitor General likes it-is to find out what the law of the nation says is piracy.
If I may, I should like to go through the history of piracy to show what happened in the Harvard draft which, was when first introduced, proposed sanctions for various forms of piracy as defined in the Harvard draft, the Geneva convention and right down to the Montreal convention. Then, I would like to refer hon. members to the treaty signed between the United States and the Republic of Cuba dealing specifically with skyjacking.
Before I speak on that, however, I should like to draw hon. members' attention and, particularly the attention of the Solicitor General, to other sections in the Criminal Code. We are now dealing with subsection (2) of section 75. Section 76 of the Criminal Code sets out various piratical acts, as they are called. Skyjacking in 1972 was referred to specifically, not in a separate section under the Criminal Code, but in subsections under section 76 dealing with piracy. I am referring to section 76.1, 76.2, and 76.3. I suggest that that was a very natural section for the government to amend when it wanted to have more severe penalties with regard to skyjacking because they knew that under the laws of nations skyjacking is an integral part of piracy. So where else would you amend the Criminal Code but simply under the piracy sections?
The reason I raise this point is that I think we must then read section 75 and all of 76, including the skyjacking provisions, to see their impact if the Solicitor General and the government get their wish in the amendment they are now proposing to Bill C-84. In short, they will put Canada in the position of being the most hospitable nation for skyjackers in this area of the world. In 1974, the United States Congress passed a law dealing specifically with piracy in the air, as it was called, and specifically providing for the death penalty in cases where any plane from the United States is involved. As I have said, Cuba has a treaty with the United States dealing with the question of air piracy, and as we know, Cuba is a retentionist nation. Russia, Japan, Ireland, St. Pierre and Miquelon are all retentionist. In fact, every nation around Canada is a retentionist nation, and if the minister and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) make piracy an offence punishable only by imprisonment for life, that will mean we are the most hospitable nation in this part of the world for those who would seize planes for whatever purpose.
In support of what I am saying I refer hon. members first to the Harvard Draft, which was prepared in the early 1950's. It was a draft prepared in anticipation of the Geneva Convention, and again I emphasize that I am trying to look for exactly what the law of nations is as referred to in section 75(1) with regard to piracy. In the Harvard draft under the title "Piracy"-and I emphasize that; there was no equivocation-various definitions which were used in their proposed convention were set out. Item 5 states:
The term "ship" means any water craft or air-craft of whatever size.
It goes on to mention, for example, that a ship may retain its national character although it has become a pirate ship, and that the retention or loss of national

character is determined by the law of the state from which it was derived. In short, it is only a draft. I simply draw hon. members' attention to the fact that in the initial draft before the Geneva Convention there was no question that piracy was something which involved not only ships on the high seas but also aircraft in the skies.
I have here the Convention of the High Seas signed in April, 1958-by Canada, incidentally-known as the Geneva Convention. It states:
All states shall cooperate to the fullest possible extent in the repression of piracy on the high seas or in any other place outside the jurisdiction of any state.
Article 15 states:
Piracy consists of any of the following acts: (a) any illegal acts of violence, detention or any act... committed for private ends by the crew or the passengers of a private ship or private aircraft, and directed (a) On the high seas, against another ship or aircraft, or against persons or property on board such ship or aircraft; (b) Against a ship, aircraft persons or property in a place outside the jurisdiction of any State;
It goes on to mention the various things which were to be included in that Geneva Convention. I re-emphasize that Canada signed that.
A refinement of the Geneva Convention was the Tokyo Convention in 1969, again signed by Canada. Incidentally, when I say that these conventions were signed, I think it is very interesting because these conventions have been signed by Canada right up to recent times, and who signs right beside us? The Republic of China. We saw fit to sign conventions dealing with piracy along with the Republic of China, but for some odd reason we are now told that in terms of Olympic sport the same Republic of China has no business using that name in Montreal. I mention that because surely that is another example of the inconsistency of this government.
Let me again go through the various conventions. On December 12, 1969 the United Nations General Assembly dealt with this question and set out that there should be severe penalties for such things as skyjacking, which comes under the general definition of piracy. The Hague Convention of 1970 was signed in December of that year and states:
Each Contracting State undertakes to make the offence punishable by severe penalties.
In that case they were referring to the offence of piracy of aircraft, or skyjacking, whichever term hon. members prefer.
The Montreal Convention was, I suppose, the last main convention signed by various states of the world touching on this subject. That convention was signed in September, 1971 and came into force in January, 1973. It specifically set out that there should be severe penalties for the kind of thing to which we are now referring, and I re-emphasize that it simply highlighted the fact that the whole question of skyjacking is simply part of an over-all international approach to attempt to halt piracy.
With that background I would now like to discuss the response of the United States. The United States as well as Canada signed the Montreal, the Hague, Tokyo and Geneva Conventions. What have the Americans decided to do with regard to air piracy? I refer hon. members to the anti-hijacking act of 1974 which provides under the head-

ing "Aircraft Piracy Outside Special Aircraft Jurisdiction of the United States" the following:
Whoever aboard an aircraft in flight outside the special aircraft jurisdiction of the United States commits 'an offense' as defined in the Convention for the Suppression of Unlawful Seizure of Aircraft. ..
That is the longer name for the Montreal Convention.
... and is afterward found in the United States shall be punished-
(A)	by imprisonment for not less than 20 years; or
(B)	if the death of another person results from the commission or
attempted commission of the offense, by death or by imprisonment
for life.
That was passed in 1974 by the Congress of the United States, and I suggest that it is comparable to the section the government now proposed to delete from the Criminal Code of Canada. The following is the government's wording as it now stands in the Criminal Code:
Every one who commits piracy while in or out of Canada is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for life, but if while committing or attempting to commit piracy he murders or attempts to murder another person or does any act that is likely to endanger the life of another person he shall be sentenced to death.
If the Criminal Code is left intact with regard to aircraft piracy or piracy on the high seas, then a law exists which is comparable to the law passed in 1974 by the Congress of the United States, I suggest in answer to the conventions the Americans signed along with Canada at Montreal, the Hague, Tokyo and Geneva.
Is it not strange that our biggest neighbour passed a law as recently as 1974 to put teeth into what they call their aircraft piracy law in the form of the death penalty while we in Canada have that provision in our Criminal Code and choose, if we follow the pattern set by the government, to delete that provision? Even if all hon. members in this House were abolitionists, surely they would not be acting responsibly if they expected Canada to become the only totally abolitionist nation in this part of the world with respect to aircraft piracy. Let us think of what will happen if this section is deleted, as the government proposes. It will mean that a person who has taken over an aircraft might deliberately direct that aircraft to be flown to Canada because he will know that there is no death penalty here.
If this section is deleted, he could execute everyone on that aircraft, and the law of the land will say that the worst penalty he will have to pay will be imprisonment for life. Is that really what even abolitionists are willing to live with? I can see some argument that if the United States, Russia, Ireland or any other country was abolitionist as far as air piracy is concerned, there would not be that kind of pressure put on Canada where we might end up with an air piracy that has nothing to do with us except that the pirates know this is a safe haven; that even if people die as a result of it, the maximum penalty the government could enforce is life imprisonment. I think that is the crux of the two motions now before us. Do we, as members, want to go that far, bearing in mind that, like it or not, this is a retentionist world, and the nations around us have chosen to say that air piracy is an offence and if death occurs as a result, the death penalty may be prescribed?
July 6, 1976

I could read various other sections of the act passed by the United States Congress which deal with this question. Section 104 states:
(1) Whoever commits or attempts to commit aircraft piracy, as herein defined, shall be punished-
"(A) by imprisonment for not less than 20 years; or "(B) if the death of another person results from the commission or attempted commission of the offence, by death or by imprisonment for life."
Again, under the heading "Procedure in respect of penalty for aircraft piracy", it reads:
(c) (1) A person shall be subjected to the penalty of death for any offence prohibited by section 902(i) or 902(n) of this act only if a hearing is held in accordance with this subsection.
It goes on to express many jury provisions, and that type of thing, which would apply in the case of someone who was being tried on charge of aircraft piracy. I raise this point because I think it is important to refute what I would suggest was the misrepresentation of the Solicitor General that somehow skyjacking is not piracy. Our own law is clear, Mr. Speaker. Subsection 1 of section 75 of the Criminal Code is not going to be changed. It makes it very clear. It reads:
Every one commits piracy who does any act that, by the law of nations, is piracy-
Note that, Mr. Speaker, "by the law of nations". I believe the Solicitor General owes it to this House to explain what he understands to be the law of nations as far as piracy is concerned.

I have cited the various conventions where this question has been dealt with. I have shown the history in some 20 years of how the various nations have interpreted and defined piracy. I think it is now up to the Solicitor General to tell this House why he believes piracy does not include skyjacking. Certainly, there is no definition in the Criminal Code that he can rely upon that would automatically say that in respect of the law of nations, piracy somehow means something different in Canada from what it means in the other nations of the world. Bearing this in mind, Mr. Speaker, I think those who have already expressed, much more ably than I have, the terror of aircraft piracy have a good point. Surely, in our rush to amend, to become an abolitionist nation, we should hesitate and look at what is happening in some other nations.
I believe, and I think I am correct, that somehow this government has become obsessed with waiting to be one of the first nations in the world to become totally abolitionist. The world is not ready for that, Mr. Speaker. The people of Canada are not ready for that. I think even the government agrees that about 80 per cent of the Canadian people believe we should retain the death penalty for at least some crimes. I think if you were to ask the people of Canada-and I would challenge the government to have a plebiscite on this-if they think the death penalty should be retained with respect to air piracy, or piracy generally, well over 80 per cent of the people would say yes.

Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. members for allowing me a few additional minutes. I will sum up by saying that I can understand abolitionist members in this House stating that they believe, in conscience, that we should do away with the death penalty. I ask them also to consider whether it is wise to do away with the death penalty with respect to an offence such as piracy, bearing in mind that piracy is not something that will occur only within the boundaries of Canada but has an international relationship. Piracy occurs on the high seas or in the air, under no direct sovereign control. Is it right that we should allow Canadians, through our Criminal Code amendments, to get out of step with the rest of the world so that Canada may become a haven for those who commit air piracy? I believe the majority of Canadians-80 per cent or more- would say no. I think those in this House who would support the government with regard to abolition for all, in the sense of ordinary crime, would stop at the crime of air piracy.
That is what is before us today, Mr. Speaker. I sincerely hope that those who up to this point have rather generally supported the government will say, on the question of air piracy, "I call a halt. I think the death penalty should be retained."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds), the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier), and the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) have argued that section 75 of the Criminal Code, which deals with piracy, also covers air hijacking or air piracy. I have said it does not, because in 1972 this House passed legislation dealing specifically with aircraft hijacking. Section 76.1 of the Criminal Code deals with the hijacking of aircraft, section 76.2 deals with endangering the safety of aircraft in flight and rendering aircraft incapable of flying, and section 76.3 deals with carrying offensive weapons or explosive substances on aircraft or putting them on aircraft. Section 75 does not deal with air piracy, because we have that very specific and particular section following it which deals with the very subject. This amendment was passed in 1972 by this House in response to the air piracy and air hijacking question at that time, following international discussion.
I have consulted the Department of Justice and am told that because we have specific sections dealing with air hijacking, these prevail over the general sections and that is the general interpretation of the law. When we passed these sections in 1972 we provided that the penalty for aircraft hijacking, endangering aircraft or pirating aircraft would be life imprisonment. I can understand some hon. members who believe in capital punishment wishing to change the penalty to death. But they would have to

July 6, 1976
Capital Punishment
propose amendments to sections 76.1, 76.2 and 76.3 of the Criminal Code. This cannot be done simply by moving a motion to strike out clause 3 of Bill C-84.
A charge was last laid under section 75 of the Criminal Code, the section we are now discussing, in 1872, in Victoria, British Columbia. Four individuals charged under that section were sentenced to death, but their sentences were commuted. That was the last time a charge under section 75, which deals with piracy involving ships, was laid in Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Some countries have changed all this.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
The hon. member suggests that some countries are applying the law relating to piracy at sea to air piracy. This would have been the case in Canada if we had not passed in 1972 specific amendments to the Criminal Code dealing with aircraft hijacking and if we had signed the convention referred to. If it were not for these provisions, the old sections on piracy would apply to air piracy as well. I am informed by the Department of Justice that we have specific provisions dealing with air hijacking, or air piracy, which are not in section 75. I am referring to section 76, the heading above which is "Offences relating to aircraft." Offences relating to aircraft are covered under the provisions of that section and not by section 75. As I say, I can appreciate some hon. members wishing to make death the penalty for air hijacking. But to achieve their purpose they would have to move amendments to section 76 and following sections of the Criminal Code.
In this bill we are merely removing the death penalty with respect to piracy involving ships, in order to be consistent with other things we are doing. Some hon. members may disagree with this, and I respect their position. I merely say that one cannot deal with the question of capital punishment for air piracy or air hijacking by amending section 75 of the Criminal Code. One would have to amend section 76 and sections following. As I have said, the last time anyone was charged under section 75 was in 1872.

Bearing in mind that Section 75(1) of the Criminal Code reads, "Every one commits piracy who does any act that, by the law of nations, is piracy," will the Solicitor General indicate why he does not believe that one can include, under the law of nations, aircraft piracy under the heading of piracy, bearing in mind the terms of the Geneva convention to which we are party and the various other conventions emanating from that convention?

As I understand it, skyjacking at present is an offence included under the general heading of piracy. I should think a strong argument could be made, if the section is left the way it is, for a skyjacker to be charged under section 75 or under the broad heading of piracy. I say that since the law of nations has made it clear that piracy includes aircraft piracy as well as piracy involving ships on the high seas. Does the Solicitor General feel that the law of nations does not include, under piracy, aircraft piracy?

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am advised-and I sought legal advice on the point-that if we had not in 1972 introduced specific provisions with respect to aircraft hijacking and offences with respect to aircraft, the hon. member's contention would prevail. We would look to the usage definition, to international custom, and so on, or we might even examine treaties to see how piracy, under section 75, might be defined. However, in Canada parliament makes the laws of the country and the laws of parliament prevail over any treaty or international usage. In this case, the particular sections which parliament has passed prevail. If we had not introduced those sections, piracy could have been interpreted, according to the legal opinion I have been given, in the way the hon. member suggests.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct one last question to the Solicitor General? Section 75 of the Criminal Code covers the occurrence of death during piracy. Is it not reasonable to say that when that happens, the ultimate offence has been committed? If you commit the offence of aircraft piracy and death occurs, you may be punished with death. On the other hand, subsections dealing with skyjacking do not refer to the situation in which death occurs. They simply say that if you make off with an aircraft, you can be sent to prison for life. Surely there is a sharp distinction to be drawn between the situation contemplated under section 75, where provision is made for the death penalty if death occurs, and the situation contemplated in section 76, where there is no suggestion of what the penalty shall be if death occurs.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to answer the hon. member's question, I am advised that anyone who causes the death of an individual on an aircraft, either deliberately or otherwise, through negligence or some act which endangers the aircraft, can be charged with murder or any substantive offence related to murder. We have checked with the Department of Justice and have learned that eight charges have been laid in Canada for aircraft hijacking since the introduction of the relevant sections in 1972.
In addition, we also amended the Aeronautics Act in 1972. I do not have those provisions before me at present. Those provisions were passed as a result of the international conferences referred to by the hon. member. Nations which signed those agreements were obligated or responsible for doing something serious about aircraft hijacking and terrorism involving aircraft. Some countries, like the United States, introduced provisions providing for the death penalty. In Canada we introduced provisions which provide for life imprisonment.
To be fair to the hon. members although I mentioned a legal opinion concerning section 75, I must confess that I

do not think it has been tested in the courts, mainly because so few charges have been laid under section 75. In other words, I do not think anyone has laid a charge under section 75, with respect to aircraft piracy, which has been challenged and tested in the courts. But the opinion is that because we have such specific sections in Canada, they cover that specific issue.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
May I put on record some figures relating to skyjacking attempts since January, 1975. Altogether there were 277 successful attempts and a total of 452 attempts. These figures show that we face a serious problem with regard to skyjacking and that such piracy is still taking place. We all know of incidents which took place in the last two weeks. One attempt was made last night. To remind hon. members, especially abolitionists, what happens when a plane is skyjacked I shall read part of a news report headlined, "Two killed, 10 hurt in Iraqi hijacking." The report says:
The pilot of an Iraqi Airlines domestic flight felt a hard object on his temple and heard a click.
"I'll blow your brains out if you don't immediately fly out of Iraq," said a man who had suddenly appeared in the cockpit.
Just imagine if that had happened to the Solicitor General's brother or to some other relative of his. How would he have liked it? How would he feel if any of his relatives were in such a position?
We should be given complete protection against these individuals and there should be swift justice in dealing with the characters who are putting guns to pilots' heads, instead of finding ways to pamper them. The intruder, wielding a pistol, was one of a trio of anti-Iraqi Kurdish hijackers aboard a Boeing 737 carrying 85 passengers and seven crew members on a flight from Baghdad to the northern town of Mosul. The pilot flew immediately to Tehran airport, ignored a refusal to land, skimmed over fire engines blocking runways, and almost flipped the plane as he brought it down on uneven, muddy ground beyond a landing strip. The first thing the hijackers did was to order $5 million ransom and the release of 85 Kurdish prisoners held in Iraq. They threatened to blow up the plane, with all aboard, if these demands were refused.
This is how the drama ended. Soon after, a shoot-out between the gunmen and Iraqi security officers on the
Capital Punishment
aircraft resulted in the death of a female passenger and one of the hijackers. Ten other persons were injured. As bullets whizzed, passengers tumbled out of the plane through an emergency exit. The two remaining hijackers jumped out of another door to surrender to Iranian authorities when they ran out of ammunition. How fortunate that they had run out of ammunition! Many people find it hard to get over incidents such as this. A lot of them are affected for the rest of their lives. This is an aspect which should be given consideration, rather than the fate of the hijackers. If it were known that swift justice would face these people, if they had realized they would be sent before a firing squad or to a gas chamber, I am sure many of them would have had second thoughts.
There was another case recently which was reported in the press under the headline, "Hijacked jet takes to air after guerrillas kill 36". The news agency reported the affair as follows:
Arab terrorists who killed at least 36 people at Rome and Athens airports began a search for a haven in the Middle East today in their hijacked West German jet liner.
After a night of terror at the Athens airport during which they are reported to have murdered four hostages, the gunmen took off with 12 hostages in the Boeing 737.
The Lebanese government refused to let them land in Beirut and they put down in Damascus, the Syrian capital.
Twenty-four hours earlier at Rome's Leonardo da Vinci airport the guerrillas had killed 30 people in a fire-bomb and machine-gun attack, the bloodiest Arab commando strike yet.
This is what is happening. This is why I hope the Solicitor General will bring in necessary amendments to the Criminal Code to enable the supreme penalty to be imposed on hijackers. In some cases these people are being treated far too leniently. Some of them have even been getting day passes. One man who hijacked a Pacific Western Airlines' plane and demanded $2 million for its safety has been placed on a pre-release program from Riverview Hospital by a provincial cabinet. I hope we are not releasing any of the other skyjackers, if there are any in custody. They should be kept behind locked doors at all times, not given weekend passes.
Here is a further instance of the danger we are encountering almost daily. I have before me a news agency story headed, "Ransom demand for jet hostages-free 53 prisoners". This is what we read:
Kampala, Uganda-Palestinian extremists have demanded the release of 53 "freedom fighters" imprisoned in Israel and four other countries in exchange for 256 hostages and a hijacked French airliner. They said severe penalties would follow if demands were not met.
France immediately said it would not give in to the guerrillas who commandeered an Air France airbus Sunday over Greece during a flight from Tel Aviv to Paris. Israel, with 40 prisoners on the list and an estimated 100 citizens being held hostage, said it has to consult. Top officials in Israel, which since 1968 has steadfastly refused to yield to terrorist demands, said they hold France responsible for the passengers.
Here is another case in which 36 people were murdered by terrorists in a hijacking. Such things happen regularly and the situation presents a growing menace. The cost of additional security measures in astronomical. For instance, the United States has had to spend more than $5 billion on extra security at airports, including the searching of passengers to ascertain whether they are carrying guns or knives.

Capital Punishment
The hon. for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) mentioned earlier the position taken by Cuba. Castro is giving every indication of being fed up to the teeth with criminal types who arrive in that country aboard commandeered U.S. aircraft. On November 15 he offered to negotiate a broad agreement which would halt the hijacking of U.S. planes to Cuba. The U.S. accepted and said talks would soon begin. The White House and Congress, after sparring over the details of a tough, new anti-hijacking law, now appear to be close to agreement. This measure would create a new federal police force to keep potential hijackers off U.S. airliners.
I understand that a strong anti-hijacking law narrowly missed passage as Congress hurried to adjourn last October. At that time most differences between Congress and the White House had been ironed out. It is now predicted that approval could come soon. Hon. members will have noted the creation of a new federal police force to deal with hijackers. This is an indication of the extreme steps which have become necessary for the protection of passengers. The cost, as I say, is astronomical. It is another important reason why we should impose the supreme penalty on skyjackers, to let them know we mean busi-nesss. It is true that many of these incidents have taken place in other parts of the world, but we should not forget that there are often Canadian passengers aboard these planes. In the recent case where the Israeli commando troops released the hostages, there were five Canadians among the passengers.
When President Nixon was in office, after the U.S. Supreme Court had ruled against the death penalty for many crimes he said he hoped the ruling did not apply to skyjacking. That ruling has, of course, been changed and the supreme penalty is applicable to skyjackers in most states. As part of the measures which have been taken to deal with hijackers, Canada and the United States have entered into certain informal agreements. Officials responsible for aircraft safety in both countries realize, as never before, that the two countries share one piece of airspace and that it is time to set up a procedure for handling transborder airplane piracy. It is too bad there is not in Canada the same penalty for hijackers as there is in the United States.
In closing, may I express the hope that the Solicitor General will reconsider his position and consult the Department of Justice in order to bring in necessary amendments to the Criminal Code to impose the supreme penalty on hijackers.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with your permission, I will of course yield the floor to the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) and I will resume right after.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to speak briefly on the motion, and I appreciate the co-operation of the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) in allowing me to speak at this time. I am not going into the discussion whether the proposed amendment dealing specifically with piracy also involves the more critical

crime of hijacking in the air which, as several members have outlined, is one of the great problems facing our civilized community at this time.
I think it can be argued, as the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) did argue, that the crime of piracy does embrace hijacking. But rather than get into the legal aspects of that problem, I would just re-emphasize that any attempt to remove capital punishment from crimes of piracy, acts of treason or, to put it in a separate category, the crime of hijacking, is contributing to the breakdown of law and order in the civilized world. I listened to the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) explaining a moment ago that this subject really is not very important since the last trial for piracy-

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: The last conviction.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
-the last conviction for piracy was in 1876, I believe was the date. So that for those who have their minds set against capital punishment there is not much danger of our carrying out the ultimate penalty for the specific crime of piracy.
What I want to debate this afternoon is the principle involved in the government's attempt to delete, as it has in a rather subtle way, the death penalty as punishment for a very serious and heinous crime. It is interesting to note that as the government of Canada, and the governments of some other countries as well, have lessened the impact of the death penalty on what we used to call capital crimes, the process of the breakdown of law and order has proceeded apace. In this country, statistics before us show that in 1967, when the subject was first debated in the House of Commons in a free vote, the vote for abolition was 105 and the vote for retention was 70. When the next vote came in 1973, the abolitionist vote was 119, to 106. The two groups were coming closer together.
In the most recent vote in the House just a couple of weeks ago, the verdict expressed by hon. members was 133 for abolition and 125 for retention. There will be two more retentionist votes, at least, when the third reading vote comes along. I will be voting for retention on the basis I put forward when I first entered this debate some weeks ago, namely, that there is an urgent need for dividing the crime of murder into the two categories of first-degree murder and second-degree murder.
I suggest that the statistical trend demonstrated by the changing vote moving more and more toward a retentionist position, is the result of an increasing wave of permissiveness in Canada, North America and Europe during the last decade or so. There has been an Increasing breakdown of law and order. Statistics for murder have doubled.
Furthermore, as the debate for abolition has gone forward, Mr. Speaker, statistics for attempted murder have not only doubled but quadrupled and a wave of violent crime, such as rape and similar acts of violence, has gone on apace, so much so that today it is one of the urgent concerns of social scientists, as expressed in some of the books heading the lists of popular publications dealing with the crime of rape. It is obvious that when the state takes a permissive attitude toward horrendous crimes of that kind, it is aiding and abetting the ultimate breakdown of law and order.
July 6, 1976

I feel sure that there would be a much larger retentionist vote but for the attitude of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his cabinet. They had to remove themselves from the principle of the free vote, which is supposed to be at the basis of this debate, and use absolute cabinet solidarity and extreme coercion to hold some of their concerned backbenchers in line. Otherwise, I am sure the vote that took place some two weeks ago would have been quite different.
I congratulate those who are carrying on this debate, even though it means sitting extra time into the summer months, because I am sure that as members opposite and some members on this side contemplate what is involved here in terms of fundamental law and order issues they, too, will change their vote when we come to the final vote on third reading.
The government itself has now become concerned at the trend toward permissiveness. It is now engaging in a tradeoff operation with its Bill C-83. It is attempting to substitute for the death penalty for deliberate, premeditated, horrendous kinds of homicide such as would be perpetrated by an act of piracy or hijacking, a mandatory life sentence for those offenders found guilty of such crimes. But as I pointed out when I spoke for the first time in this debate, this is a snare and a delusion because the government is trying to have the best of all possible worlds. The government is trying to face in two directions at once. It is emphasizing a rehabilitative and reformative posture in our penal institutions, and at the same time trading off the death penalty for a mandatory life sentence, which would make it impossible for our penal institutions to have any element of reform or rehabilitation.
This is also working against the recommendations of the law reform committee which this government appointed to consider and recommend reforms to our penal system. That committee suggests that penal institutions-largely based on statistics of increasing repetition and recidivism-have failed utterly in becoming institutions of reform and rehabilitation. The committee's recommendation to the government is that sentences for criminal activity of all kinds be reduced, rather than expanded. Notwithstanding this recommendation which is already before the government, the government is proposing a mandatory life sentence which would be a living death much harsher than the death penalty itself.
To anyone who has been abroad in recent weeks it is interesting to hear the reaction of people in other countries regarding the debate taking place on peace, order and good government, that is, Bill C-83, and this bill, C-84. With tongue in cheek they ask Canadians why Canada is begin-ing to sound more and more like a banana republic regarding law and order measures. If we remove the absolute penalty for the crime of treason, the ultimate crime against the state, and if we remove the death penalty for the crime of piracy or hijacking as the government is proposing to do, we are leaving ourselves wide open to all the terror and violence that is proliferating in the world today. No wonder Canadians travelling abroad are being asked why we are moving away from the reputation as the true north, strong and free, to a Canada which acts more like a banana republic.
Capital Punishment
In view of the crime which took place in the past week and its spectacular denouement at the airport in Uganda over the weekend, if the government persists in this doctrinaire approach-and it is doctrinaire because it is an approach not related to any facts or statistics or anything that might be based on reality-and in removing the power of the state to deal decisively with violent crime on an international scale, then instead of being known as the banana republic of North America we will become known as the Uganda of North America. We will be leaving ourselves wide open to the rising incidence of crime that is causing so much concern around the world today.
I would urge hon. members, as they contemplate this amendment, to consider that it provides them, particularly backbenchers on the government side who are of two minds, to express their concerns. They are concerned over the breakdown in law and order and the increasing trend toward immorality. This amendment does provide them with that opportunity, and I trust they will have the courage of their convictions and support it.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is not the first time I rise on the issue of capital punishment, for it has been on the order paper quite a few times since I have had the honour to represent the residents of Bellechasse in the House.
However, in previous debates I wanted to express my views objectively on this serious issue and I must say that until now I found no valid reason to change my mind on the matter. This being said, I must sincerely admit that the whole Canadian nation is watching with much interest and attention the debates being held in the House on Bill C-84, which proposes many amendments to the Criminal Code. All members will certainly agree with me that the House is under pressure as all Canadians are, for this is a very serious topic and we must take all the possible steps and use all the possible means to avoid any mistake which would be detrimental to an individual who, by mistake or by profession, would have committed the serious crime of taking the life of another person.
Mr. Speaker, while the news media seem less interested in this matter at this time, the fact remains that public attention is still focused on the proceedings at the report stage and in the proposed amendments to Bill C-84. Everyone is concerned about the real meaning to be considered when it comes to evaluating the responsibilities of an individual within Canadian society.
What are the responsibilities of an individual towards another? What must invite him to respect the rights of another, specifically his right to live as an individual? At the family level, what are the responsibilities of the head of the family? On what grounds can an individual take the life of the head of a family-man or woman-who bears responsibilities for the children both parents wanted to have and who had met their responsibilities and done their duties during the normal course of their life?
At the municipal level, what are our responsibilities? As many members in this House, I had the opportunity once in my life to play a role at the municipal level and all those who have worked in municipal politics did so because they were dedicated to society and although they were some-

July 6, 1976
Capital Punishment
time criticized and even threatened they still accepted to take their responsibilities and the same applies at the provincial level. All hon. members, all ministers, all provincial officials have responsibilities which they must fulfill but, as far as we are specifically concerned today, it is our duty as members of the Canadian Parliament to represent the population in the highest authority that exists in our country, I mean the Canadian Parliament.
Mr. Speaker, my colleague from Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) proposed an amendment to Bill C-84, which I have the honour of supporting. I want to defend it objectively, to explain why we were prompted to move this amendment and I want to ask my colleagues of the House to adopt it so that, in the future, the Canadian population can say to me: Here is a Parliament which has fulfilled its responsibilities. The members have adopted a bill providing for penalties against those who do not want to respect the lives of their fellow beings and who do not want to abide by the true code of liberty and of respect for the lives of their fellow beings.
Mr. Speaker, clause 3 of Bill C-84 says:
"(2) Every one who commits piracy while in or out of Canada is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for life."
It does not say that the court must condemn this person to life imprisonment but rather:
... is liable to imprisonment for life."
Consequently, before the court, if that person has been guilty of an act of piracy, if the court decides to condemn him to life imprisonment, if, of course, he is found guilty, he must serve his sentence.
We must maintain the current law which the legislators before us passed after considerable thought, in other words maintain the status quo as concerns subsection 75(2) of the existing legislation which reads as follows:
Every one who commits piracy while in or out of Canada is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for life-
And it goes on because we know that the legislators at that time surely knew that some other acts were added to that which is studied in the subsection. And so it goes:
-but if while committing or attempting to commit piracy he murders or attempts to murder another person or does any act that is likely to endanger the life of another person-
... and the law says ...
... he shall be sentenced to death.
I suppose that the legislators who sat in this House and enacted the law I just quoted were intelligent and responsible people. If at that time those persons seriously assumed their responsibilities and if they included that provision in the Criminal Code it was to ensure the greatest security of the Canadian people against criminals whose vocation is to deny the rights of other citizens, particularly their right to life.
Mr. Speaker, this is why my colleague the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) and I decided to ask the House to maintain the status quo and I urge the Solicitor General to give a second thought to the wording of Bill C-84 relating precisely to that question of piracy.

In the Larousse dictionary to which I referred this morning, I checked the meaning of the word "piracy". I understand that the Larousse dictionary is not published every year. I understand that the people responsible for defining the words in the French language thought that the idea of piracy applied particularly to sea transportation because at that time, the other means of transport had not yet been invented. Those responsible for defining the words dealt only with navigation. We can read the following:
Pirate: Adventurer who practices brigandage on the high seas.
Here is a second idea:
Any man who gets rich through pillage or robbery.
These days, we know that there are thousands of such pirates who get rich through legal or illegal pillage, and who get rich through legal or illegal robbery. I have often had the opportunity in the House to denounce the legalized pillage allowed by our statutes through which certain organizations can rob individuals, society, the whole population of Canada, by the means which are placed at their disposal. Mr. Speaker, I would like to mention that it is one o'clock.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs and it is about the government's conduct with regard to the International Olympic Committee which, I wish to add, does not raise questions about Canada's policy towards China, but about our integrity as the host for the 1976 Olympics. July 6, 1976

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring your attention to a question I asked at page 3625 of Hansard for February 25, 1975, when Your Honour replied regarding the answering of starred questions in a given length of time. Your Honour indicated that the question could be left unanswered ad infinitum, at the discretion of the minister.
The purpose of starred questions, as I understand it and as the system has developed by custom over the years, is to inhibit lengthy questions with a preamble, to put them on the order paper and star them. Another purpose is to give the minister time to prepare a more complete answer than he could on the spur of the moment and, hopefully, improve the answer. This was my understanding and my reason, over the months that have elapsed since February 25, 1975, for writing to the President of the Privy Council and speaking to him on three occasions. I also felt it would give protection to the Speaker since he stated, quite cor-

July 6, 1976
Order Paper Questions
rectly, that he has no authority over starred questions as to when, if ever, they should be answered.
I also want to add that when I was ruled out of order on an oral question in a previous parliament, a former Speaker told me that my question was too long, that he was trying to contain the length of questions and answers so as to get to as many members as possible, and therefore my question should be starred and put on the order paper and it would be answered within a few days. This is, and has been, my understanding of the status of starred questions.
In the mother of parliaments a starred question is answered within two full days. In Canada it appears we are a bit unorthodox. Originally, as I understand it, only written questions were admissible by the Standing Orders and had to appear on the order paper. Then the asking of oral questions became customary on the basis of extreme urgency, and this has now become firmly established. As a matter of fact, Sir Herbert Williams probably asked about
4,000	questions during his parliamentary career, and described questions asked in the House as perhaps one of the most powerful instruments of democracy.
Nothing could more weaken the control of parliament over the executive than the abolition or curtailment of the right of a member of parliament to ask a question in the House of Commons. It is my contention that starred questions, by custom, should be given their useful place between oral questions and written questions.
I want to thank you, Mr. Speaker, and the House for the indulgence in listening to my plea to retain a useful tool in the armament of democracy and to strengthen the hand of every member of parliament by placing starred questions in the place in which custom has already placed them.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CANADIAN COAST GUARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to reinforce what has been said so well by my colleague, the hon. member for Simcoe North. In the past it has been recognized and accepted by all sides that starred questions had a high degree of urgency. I notice that some on the order paper are simple ones that have been there since April. They are not particularly embarrassing. As a matter of fact, the hon. member for Fundy-Royal has one which asks what the regulations are concerning spouses accompanying officers to functions in an officers' mess. This question was asked early in May, and it is still outstanding.
I do not think any question that goes on the order paper with a star should take more than a week or ten days to answer. Certainly, with today's communications, there is no excuse for delay. Any question with a star, which has a privileged position and asks that the parliamentary secretary or the minister concerned should read the answer aloud, should be, by courtesy, answered within a working week. If it appears on Monday, it should be read aloud by the following Monday.
I would hope the Chair would assist the House in seeing that the regulation is enforced, not by order, but there is not inconsiderable moral suasion available to the Chair-a matter about which I know something.
(Mr. Rynard.]

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: CANADIAN COAST GUARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I understand it, questions are starred simply in order to obtain an oral reply. There is no indication in the star itself that the matter ought to be answered with any greater urgency than any other question on the order paper. Your Honour has always held, as have your predecessors, that questions ought to be placed on the order paper if they are not of such an urgent nature as to be asked during the oral question period at the beginning of each day's sitting.
If my hon. friends have some precedents that they want to communicate to me, I would be glad to hear them. I listened with interest to the intervention of the hon. member for Edmonton West. I am not aware of any precedent of Your Honour or your predecessors to the effect that starred questions ought to be answered with more celerity than questions on the order paper that are not starred. I am ready, as my hon. friend has indicated, to be instructed by members with more experience, and I would welcome any assistance he can offer. Of course, I did not hear that assistance in his intervention before Your Honour.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: CANADIAN COAST GUARD
speechtext:
The matter raised by the hon. member for Simcoe North has been raised before, as he indicated, and he had the conversations alluded to in his remarks today with the hon. President of the Privy Council concerning this matter. I think it is clear that in the past there has certainly been that impression among some hon. members, even if it was never enshrined, and it certainly has never been enshrined in the customs of the House, which are equally as important as our Standing Orders. If that has not been the custom or practice of the House, it certainly has been the impression in the minds of a good many members that it was so.
A cursory examination of the precedents verifies there is no regulatory force behind the notion that there should be a time limit with respect to answering starred questions. However, since we have the oral question period in which we attempt to accommodate questions which are sufficiently urgent to warrant exposure during that time, since ordinary questions on the order paper can be answered within a greater period of time, and since we have starred questions which demand an oral answer, there is support for the idea that the urgency of the starred question which must be answered orally lies between that of oral questions and questions on the order paper. But there is no indication in the precedents or practices of this House that that has ever been formalized.
It is hoped that some understanding can be reached with respect to starred questions. It might be urged that the procedure committee should examine this question in the course of its re-examination of the procedures of the House. Members who have participated in such discussions on previous occasions are distinguished members of that committee. It would be helpful if the committee could examine this matter specifically to see whether some recommendation could be made to allow a clearer understanding to be reached about the degree of urgency which might be attached to starred questions.
I have asked a study to be undertaken in my office to determine with greater clarity the exact experience of the House in the recent past. When the study is complete,
July 6, 1976

perhaps I can supply copies of it to members of the procedure committee and others who are interested, to see whether it might form the basis of suggestions to be made by that committee.

Mr. Speaker, I think what has been said effectively closes the matter. I suggest to the President of the Privy Council that it would be helpful if he would consider the position of the government with respect to starred questions before the committee deals with the matter. Perhaps on an experimental basis we could institute a temporary, voluntary system with respect to how starred questions are to be dealt with in future.
I was rising on another point of order to do with a practice which has developed concerning the recognition by members of this House, other than yourself, of distinguished visitors to Canada who may be in one of the galleries of the House. I am not suggesting that distinguished visitors to our country who are in our galleries ought not to be recognized, but I say to you, sir, that we do those visitors a great disservice and discourtesy if, as was the case with the group from the European parliament today, they are recognized by someone other than yourself during a controversial portion of the question period. Perhaps the Secretary of State for External Affairs thought it would be appropriate to recognize our distinguished visitors during the question period.
To the extent that this occurred during the parliamentary struggle known as the question period when some matters hit close to the bone, I am prepared to accept it, but I suggest it was bad manners. It is bad manners for parliament and improper on the part of all of us to allow this situation to continue. Sir, if official visitors to this House are to be recognized, you, and only you, as the first commoner of this House, ought to call the attention of members and to the public generally, through the press, to the presence in the gallery of distinguished visitors to our country.
I think it is extremely important that recognition on such occasions should not be regarded as legitimate government recognition, or legitimate opposition recognition, but as parliamentary recognition. If the visitors are so distinguished that they ought to be recognized, then you, and only you, sir, ought to do the recognizing. That course, I suggest, would be more conducive to order and decorum in this House and to the proper operation of the question period. I repeat, if the visitors are so distinguished, if the delegation is so prestigious as to warrant recognition by this House, you, sir, as the first commoner, ought to recognize our visitors on behalf of all members of the House of Commons. I ask Your Honour to take that matter into consideration.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before the lunch recess, I was presenting arguments explaining why I support the motion of my colleague the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin).
Before, if I may do so, I would like to thank the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Dupras) for supporting the motion which I presented at the opening of this sitting and I would also like to thank all hon. members of the House who supported it unanimously, in order to clarify once for all the days of sitting of Parliament when it comes to St. John the Baptist Day or Dominion Day. I thank you all very much.
Mr. Speaker, as amendment No. 10 deals with clause 3 of Bill C-84 and as it concerns piracy, I have been a little bit surprised when I heard the Solicitor General who, apparently, wants to have us understand that, in the spirit of the bill, the word "piracy" applies especially to air piracy. However, it is not referred to at all as the bill simply says "piracy". As my colleague from Lotbiniere explained very clearly yesterday when he took part in the debate, there are other acts of piracy just as criminal as air piracy and which, to my mind, should have the same consequences for those who commit them.
When we read the history of our country or the history of the world, we remember those novels about piracy on the seas, when people would join the crew of a ship to seize it, to sail it away from its destination and to take hold of its cargo to make a fortune. Nowadays, there is a new form of piracy. During these last few years, we have experienced many aircraft hijackings which claimed many victims. All nations in the world concerned about the protection of air passengers were shocked by hostage takings and sometimes by killings of innocent victims. Mr. Speaker, I remember and I think all hon. members also remember this kind of piracy which was the subject of international conference discussions on air piracy to find ways to stem this epidemic of crimes.
Everyone will recall that parliamentarians of various countries advocated very severe penalties for criminals who hijacked planes away from their destination and kept a number of passengers as hostages to gain personal benefits.
Mr. Speaker, this kind of hijacking is still going on. Although we in Canada never had the misfortune of being in such a situation, it does not mean that in the coming months or years such a situation will not occur.
