Mr. Speaker, my intervention at this time will not be as lengthy as some in the past. I find in clause 3 an amending section dealing with the subject of piracy and a distinction is drawn in section 75(2) of the Criminal Code. Not only does that section speak of committing an act of piracy within or without Canada, but it goes further and provides that if an individual or individuals, while committing piracy or attempting to commit piracy, murders or attempts to murder or does any act likely to endanger the life of another person, then the wrongdoer shall be sentenced to death. In the present bill provision is only made for a person who commits piracy while in or without Canada; there is nothing about attempted piracy.
I suppose the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) might answer, "Oh well, we would lay a charge, in the ordinary course of events, either of murder or attempted murder". But what are we to do in this day and age about the modern version of an act of piracy of the kind we saw last week and two announced even this morning? I suppose Canadians will say that these things happen in other lands. One might almost expect those high moralists who talk of the abolition of capital punishment to say that such acts are committed in barbaric or less civilized lands. I say nonsense, Mr. Speaker. It is just as conceivable to have an aircraft hijacked in Greece, Israel, France or Germany. The United States had a rash of hijackings and we have had a couple, and I think we may yet see further attempts at hijacking or actual hijacking of aircraft into or out of Canada take place.
When hijackings occur, people do get murdered. These people are not only security agents but passengers. I would want a much more valid explanation than the one I have been able to cull from these amendments in Bill C-84 or from the testimony of the Solicitor General's officials before the justice and legal affairs committee. Simply to say that piracy will merit a life sentence does not satisfy me. Clause 5 of the bill repeals section 218 of the Criminal Code and substitutes the following;
(2) For the purposes of Part XX, the sentence of imprisonment for life prescribed by this section is a minimum punishment.
I gather from the popular impression that this minimum punishment is 25 years. It is hard to determine whether there will be an application for parole permitted at the end of 25 years or whether it will be at the end of 18 years; I
Capital Punishment
rather suspect it will be the latter. I think, as I said last night, that in this modern day it is far crueller to consign a man or woman to the Bastille, as they were in the eighteenth century in France, to be put away, forgotten, pigeonholed as just another file that the Solicitor General's department will occasionally examine in a raw of other files.
One has to undergo incarceration or restriction of liberty to know what it is like. I hate to be subjective about this, because somehow I feel that subjectivity may not be the best attitude to take in arriving at a judgment in such matters as these. However, one is conditioned by one's circumstances, and I can assure hon. members that nearly three years of very severe restriction of my freedom during World War II, knowing of those who had to suffer solitary confinement for real or imagined wrongs against the captive power, did much to the morale of prisoners of war.
If there is no hope, and release from prison is 25 years down the road, then, notwithstanding the relative comforts of the modern-day prison compared to the Bastille, this is an invitation by society to the individual to remove or do away with himself. Certainly, there will be no hope of rehabilitation because that person will in the normal course of events reach middle or old age, if he should survive the sentence of 25 years at all. As I say, why not park them all in a mausoleum right away because they will become as the living dead.
There are a few people who are sentenced now to terms of 25 years hard labour, although very rarely, who have the propect, if they behave, of being up for parole at the end of one-third of their sentence. A man of 25 years of age sentenced to 25 years may expect, if he meets the other conditions-and they are stringent-to get out on parole in eight or nine years. What a difference between eight or nine years and what is proposed! This provides a goal to work toward, which is not inherent in 25-year or perhaps an 18-year sentence. These people will become, if this should be Canada's law, the living dead. I do not know whether society is any further ahead when it says to a man or woman in the courts that he or she is sentenced to a living death, or is sentenced to suffer death by hanging. One is quicker and very sure, whereas the other takes much longer but is equally sure.
For these reasons, I do not see what improvement there is in the amendment contained in Bill C-84. My colleague, the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds), has moved that clause 3 be deleted and, in effect, that section 75(2) of the Criminal Code be maintained. I am in full support of his amendment and I commend it to the House.

Mr. Speaker, I must admit that there might be some hon. members who at first glance at this amendment to delete clause 3 might think it has some validity because you can talk about piracy in connection with a navy if you have a navy, but if your navy is non-existent, you can no longer talk about that form of piracy. The bill would become redundant in that sense. Considering the condition of our navy, it may be that the bill would be redundant in that regard. Therefore, I cannot understand why this morning the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) argued that the bill would have an effect only in the matter of piracy on the high seas. When we look at the two or three ships which are left in our navy, I do not know why any pirate would want to take any of them. The object of piracy is to get to port, and if a pirate were to seize one of our ships on the high seas the question is whether he would be caught long before he got to port.
At first glance, there might be some hon. members who think there is some validity in the government's bill and that we should eliminate the death penalty for piracy. However, it has always been contended that piracy should be deemed an invasion of the country whose flag a ship is flying, and throughout history an act of piracy has been considered an invasion of the integrity of the country to which the ship in question belonged. In addition to that, there is the vulnerable position of the people on board ship who are not in easy contact with their government and are isolated from the help of their compatriots and their government's constabulary forces. Piracy has been considered throughout history as the ultimate act of vandalism and a fraudulent affront to the integrity of governments.
Whenever we board an Air Canada jet, we walk past our country's coat of arms emblazoned on the fuselage of the aircraft. To me, that is a pretty clear indication that our government is fundamentally involved in the airlines of our country. That is our indication that unlawful intrusion of that aircraft is piracy.
In any act of war, the most heinous by-product is the anguish suffered by innocent bystanders. We can look back at the record of the suffering and anguish, especially on the part of women and children, in the Second World War during the Battle of Britain, the air raids over Germany and the bombing of Hiroshima. It is the suffering by innocent bystanders that is the most heinous aspect of war. How much worse is it when there is nowhere to hide? There have been cases in wartime when mass evacuation has taken place. We remember well that during the Battle of Britain thousands of women and children were taken out of London to the countryside, and many of them were brought to Canada.
However, what do innocent bystanders do if they are in mid-air on an aircraft flying at 35,000 feet? They are locked into the cabin of that aircraft. When a government authorizes or licenses a ship or a plane to carry the general public,
July 6, 1976

it owes the public the protection it deserves. In its present form, this bill proposes to make pirates or skyjackers nothing more than we would consider prisoners of war to be. They can declare war on this country and all we will do is imprison them; and in its present form imprisonment in this country is fairly comfortable. As the present prison system operates, that would be about as effective as "Sta-lag 13" where the prisoners go in and out at will. I am not implying that the administrators of our penitentiaries are the counterparts of Colonel Klink, but I am saying that the kind of support being provided by the Solicitor General makes it appear that way.
I must refer again to what the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) alluded to a few minutes ago. One of the reasons there is a rash of skyjacking in the world is that there are other terrorists in prisons and they become the reward for skyjackers. They are always the reason another skyjacking takes place. Just a few minutes ago the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) referred to the perverted sense of morality of skyjackers which involves the matter of identity and simple self-expression. It is suggested that all these people are trying to do is express themselves. There is some truth in that. In their perverted morality, these people have borrowed from the philosophy of Karl Marx, Sartre and Camus and said they are trying to express their authentic selves, and anyone trying to prevent their doing so is committing another act of immorality. They claim they are entitled to express themselves. There is no such thing, in this kind of perverted morality, as an absolute right or wrong; therefore the skyjacking of a plane is no different to these people than helping the poor.
In this country we are faced with the eventuality of having pirates or skyjackers in our prisons. The time will come when one of our planes will be skyjacked and the people in our prisons will be the reason for that skyjacking. Under the system that operates presently in this country, the next skyjackers will be rewarded for their terrorism. Allmand) cause to reconsider the definition of piracy. I share the view of piracy in this context and particularly the manner in which it is described in the Criminal Code which in section 75.1 reads:
Every one commits piracy who does any act that, by the law of nations, is piracy.
It is true, as the Solicitor General said, that the last conviction for piracy in this country was in 1867. During the past century there have been many developments in technology and in attitudes toward the law. I am satisfied in my own mind that should an incident of piracy affecting an aircraft take place, a judge could easily interpret this as meaning aircraft.
I have had other thoughts on this particular section, however, and I should like to draw to the attention of the House some anomalous situations which have developed as a result of the government's decision to include clause 3 in Bill C-84. I am convinced that as they were drawing up the bill and overflowing with this notion that they were going to eliminate the death penalty from Canadian law, they put their staff to work to find those sections of the Criminal Code where the death penalty occurred. In section 75.2 there is the possibility of someone being sentenced to death for having committed, or attempted to commit piracy although, as the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) pointed out earlier, any reference to a murder being committed in the course of committing that piracy was left out. No one will ever know why this occurred. In my opinion, it is another instance of extremely bad drafting.
Does piracy refer only to piracy on the high seas? I find it difficult to understand that the theft of a Canadian ship is the only act which can be considered a piratical act, when there are so few Canadian ships-unless we are talking about our neighbour's canoe up at the lake, or his sloop. Is that a Canadian ship? Is it piracy, or is it theft, to take charge of our neighbour's ship during the summertime? I think we have to be careful here.
In the course of eliminating the death penalty there is a most outrageous anomaly that has come to light in my study of the various related legislation on the statute books and that which is being proposed. Paragraph 76 defines piratical acts. I draw special attention to subsection (c), as follows:
76. Every one who, while in or out of Canada . . .
(c) does or attempts to do a mutinous act on a Canadian ship .. . is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for 14 years.
So a mutinous act is one of those acts which under the Criminal Code provides for imprisonment for life. In section 53 of the Criminal Code, inciting mutiny is dealt with. That is another act which, if committed, would make a person liable to imprisonment for 14 years. But mutiny itself is another matter and is referred to in sections 69 and 70 of the National Defence Act. This is where the government is carrying out a great con game. It has presented this bill as measure to eliminate capital punishment in Canada. Either it is deliberately conning the Canadian public, or its staff's work has been faulty. Section 69 of the National Defence Act reads:
Every person-

July 6, 1976
Capital Punishment
This deals with every person, not a military person.
-who joins in a mutiny that is accompanied by violence is guilty of an offence and on conviction is liable to suffer death or less punishment.
Section 70 reads:
Every person who joins in a mutiny-
It explains that he suffers something unless he is the ringleader of the mutiny, and then he shall suffer death. My purpose is to warn the abolitionists in this House that if they think by voting for this bill, including the retention of this particular amendment, they are going to see the elimination of the death penalty in Canada, they have been had-completely and utterly had. I warn them: the death penalty remains on the statute books of this country. If they go away believing that by voting for this bill they will see the end of it, they delude themselves. The government either acquiesces in perpetrating this delusion or has been extremely inept in allowing it to happen. That is all I want to say. I shall leave it to the judgment of parliament.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak on the proposed amendments to the Criminal Code regarding piracy. I will speak particularly about air piracy and kidnapping and murder associated with such acts.

Although I have no formal notes to which I may refer, I feel strongly on the subject and think I have some capacity for speaking on it. I refer to a letter sent by the Reverend Sorley, of Stouffville, Ontario. In it he raises six points. His sixth point reads in part as follows:
Let us extend the death penalty.
We should include all those who are guilty of kidnapping, terrorism, hijacking, bombing and treason. If we do, it will have a discouraging effect on any lawbreakers and bring about a reduction in every form of crime. We have, in practice, abolished the death penalty for the last thirteen years and we have an increase in crime such as never has been known in the history of Canada.
What the clergyman said in his letter cannot but make one reflect on the enormous costs which have been inflicted on Canadian taxpayers and those of other nations for implementing methods which help to prevent acts of terrorism in the air. Canadians employed in security duties at airports and near aircraft could be better and more constructively employed elsewhere, at considerably less expense to the travelling public. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), in his wisdom, has developed the "user pay" concept and applied it to Canadian airports. The "user pay" policy applies not only to those operating light aircraft; it applies as well to commercial airlines, the travelling public and the long-suffering Canadian taxpayer.
I wonder what life in Canada or in any western country would be like without the embarrassment and harassment of airport security. I am thinking of what happens when an impatient air traveller is confronted by an equally impatient security officer. But it seems that most Canadians accept this new way of life, this new way of travelling, this new type of harassment, this further infringement upon civil liberties, as necessary. They look on security measures as measures to protect life and limb.
Perhaps members of parliament are more equipped than others to comment on the air piracy aspects of the bill. Many of us return frequently to our ridings at the Canadian taxpayers' expense. It takes me five or six hours of flying time to return to my western Canadian constituency. During my travels I have the opportunity to visit and observe Canadians of all walks of life. In the aircraft I see mothers with babies, aged parents and grandparents travelling to weddings, perhaps to funerals, or on holiday and I think about what can happen in the air if an act of terrorism takes place. I shudder at the consequences of air piracy.
Consider what happened recently in Uganda. All the free world lauded and applauded the actions of the Israelis in rescuring the victims of terrorism. What a frightening experience that must have been. Surely it has burned itself into the minds of all those hostages. They were held, I might add, with the apparently tacit approval of Uganda. I recall reading the reported remarks of one hostage who said, "When we heard the guns firing and the explosions, we thought it was all over for us, that our time had come."
In modern-day flying there are no second chances in the air when acts of piracy occur. Because of the ignorance, the madness of those who are involved in such acts, it takes only one mishap, one wrong move to send an aircraft plummeting to the ground. I recall an aircraft which was blown up some years ago over northern British Columbia. The identity of the perpetrator of the act was suspected; he could not be name for lack of proof. Mr. Speaker, there was
July 6, 1976

an explosion in the air; the people in the tail section were blown out of the aircraft. Actually, the entire tail section separated from the fuselage, and in a dramatic effort to save the lives of his passengers, the pilot, with enormous skill given to him by God, flew the aircraft in a flat spin right down to the ground. When the wreckage was examined, it was found that the seats had dented the floor of the aircraft only by a quarter of an inch. That shows the lightness of the impact. The pilot brought the aircraft down without the tail, without any rudders to control it, using the throttles to operate the engines on the port and starboard side. He was able to bring the aircraft relatively safely to the ground. Unfortunately, on impact the gasoline tanks exploded and all on board were incinerated.
This sort of thing has happened in Canada and is going on in the world. We hear these things almost daily. It is the new trend. Terrorists kidnap and hijack for political or financial reasons. Without doubt, such acts are premeditated. No one boards an aircraft with the idea of flying from Ottawa to Vancouver and, on arrival at Calgary, thinks it might be a good idea to hijack the aircraft. These people know what they are doing. I say that those who are prepared to inflict their criminality, their murderous intent upon Canadians deserve only one penalty, that is, the supreme penalty. This is why I support the amendment.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make some comments on this motion, one which would in effect delete clause 3 from the bill and retain the death penalty as a deterrent to acts of piracy. In today's world we do not often hear about piracy on the high seas. We hear a lot about piracy of trucks and aircraft. Piracy on the high seas has pretty well come to an end, at least on a large scale; but piracy of aircraft is something else again.
I had an experience several years ago when I was travelling on business from Madrid to London. It was a BEA flight. We were on board, and shortly before the aircraft was ready to leave the terminal, airport officials boarded high government officials from Spanish Morocco. I was sitting in the first-class section and I was shuffled out into the economy section. Incidentally, I never did get back the difference in fare, but that is beside the point. The aircraft began to taxi out to the main runway for take-off. But just before we got to the main strip, the aircraft was halted, the engines were shut down and all the passengers were taken off. The aircraft was surrounded by security people.
Airport officials brought up a vehicle, which we found out later to be a bomb disposal vehicle. All luggage was unloaded and all passengers were required to identify their luggage from behind a steel plate, after which their luggage was examined and placed in another location. When this process had been completed there were three pieces of luggage left, and we found later that those three pieces of luggage contained explosives. It was evidently the intention of somebody to blow up the aircraft. We could only surmise that it was due to the presence of the Spanish Moroccan government officials who were on board. It certainly was not because I was on board, because I was only a lowly Canadian businessman travelling abroad, trying to sell something and make a few dollars.
Capital Punishment
I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that it was a frightening experience. We did not realize what was happening until it was all over. The aircraft was taken back to the terminal and checked again, after which those of us who wished to go on to London were allowed to board. I had some urgent appointments and consequently decided to proceed. Halfway into the flight all of us were suffering from a case of jitters, wondering whether they had really got all the explosives out. This illustrates the type of risk which travellers increasingly face today and which prompt one to ask whether we ought not to retain the supreme penalty for such crimes.
In the United States, acts of piracy on board aircraft with the object of securing money seem to have diminished sharply in number. It is true that some small aircraft are hijacked, but commercial aircraft have not been endangered recently in this way. In the last few years, though, we have seen a new threat: aircraft are being hijacked not for money but for political reasons. One group of individuals differs from another on political or religious grounds and is prepared to seize an aircraft and threaten people on board, most of whom they do not know, placing their lives in jeopardy in addition to the lives of the crew, not to mention an extremely expensive piece of machinery.
I notice that our airport surveillance arrangements are manned more extensively. At the Toronto international airport there are as many as five people who take passengers through the security gates. I do not know how much this costs Canada, but I estimate it amounts to hundreds of millions of dollars a year, all paid for by the travelling public. The cost worldwide must be in the billions of dollars and all we seem to be doing is putting our trust in an electronic device.
Only a few cases involving air piracy have been tried in Canada. There was one here in Ontario, I believe, and two in British Columbia. The person who tried to hijack an Air Canada plane in Ontario was given a relatively short prison sentence, one of those tried on the west coast was given a suspended sentence, and the other was fined $100. I do not believe we can continue to accept the taking of hostages, placing in jeopardy the lives of innocent people, without specifying that this is a crime which warrants the most serious penalty which can be prescribed. I certainly do not believe that 25 years in prison, with provision for review of sentence after 15 years, is adequate.
For these reasons I shall support the motion when it comes to a vote, which I understand will be on Thursday at 9.30 p.m. or thereabouts, in the hope that the House will make it clear that piracy on aircraft in flight is a most serious matter and we must take the most severe action we can to deter it. I recall some years ago checking with Lloyds of London respecting losses in connection with aircraft they had insured throughout the world. This loss came to hundreds of millions of dollars. Insurance rates for aircraft have increased, adding to the operating cost of airlines. Of course this cost is ultimately passed on to the user of that mode of transportation.
I ask members to contemplate this motion very carefully, not just carelessly to wave it aside, saying that it is proposing the retention of capital punishment in some

July 6, 1976
Capital Punishment
form for certain crimes and they cannot support it. It would be a good thing if those members who oppose the motion were able to talk to some of the hostages in the recent incident in Uganda, to listen to their experiences and discover their feelings. I suggest they would realize that we should not lightly pass this matter off but should retain the most severe penalty that we have for the act of piracy of an aircraft.
That is about the extent of the remarks I wish to make. I will be speaking to other amendments that come forward but I thought it worth while to put on record the personal experience I had on an aircraft that was going to be blown up in the air. It was an experience I should not like to have again and which I would not wish on anybody else. I urge hon. members when considering this motion to think it out carefully and to support the deletion of clause 3 from Bill C-84.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too should like to go on record as urging all hon. members to consider favourably the motion now before the House to delete clause 3 of the bill. Clause 3 clearly states that everyone who commits piracy is liable to imprisonment for life. The hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) made a very good speech on this subject before lunch, and I was slightly amazed during the question period to hear the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) say that the legal opinion that he had received was over the telephone. Not being a lawyer but as one who has been around here for a while, I thought legal opinions were written documents that clearly spelt out in every detail the arguments for or against a given position. Yet the minister suggests that piracy applies only to ships, I assume because somebody in the justice department advised him over the telephone that that was his interpretation of section 75(1) of the Criminal Code.
Section 75(1) clearly states that everyone commits piracy who does any act that by the law of nations constitutes piracy. The Geneva conference stated that air piracy exists and is considered as such. What we are dealing with in this bill is piracy, whether it be of ships or aircraft. Piracy is the taking of a vehicle, vessel or aircraft, and endangering the lives of the people thereon.
I think there is hardly anyone in Canada, except for the scattered few in the cabinet who are obeying the dictates of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who does not believe that we should retain the death penalty for hijackers. This is what the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds) is seeking. A hijacking took place some years ago in Calgary by a person who is now serving a jail sentence. He has clearly stated that had he known that the death penalty would be invoked if someone had come to harm, he believes it would have deterred him from hijacking an aircraft, having it flown to Montana and back again to Canada. However, in that case no one lost their life and all were very fortunate.
The very essence of hijacking is that it endangers lives. Section 75(2) of the Criminal Code provides that anyone who commits or attempts to commit piracy, and who murders or attempts to murder in the course thereof, shall be sentenced to death. That is the section that Bill C-84 seeks to delete from the Criminal Code and in its place substitute life imprisonment for the death penalty.
(Mr. Kempling.]
Someone pointed out earlier today that imprisonment for life does not mean that. A person can get out of jail on guarded leave, which only means that he has to report in every so many hours while out on a week end pass. That really is not good enough. A hijacking could take place even in that short space of time. I urge all hon. members to take their obligations as members of parliament and representatives of their constituencies very seriously. This is not a complicated matter but one that is simple and straightforward. The question is: should one who causes bodily injury to another while committing an act of piracy face the supreme sentence of death?
I believe we have to make a concerted effort to cut down aircraft hijackings. The recent incident in Uganda which resulted in the freeing of 100 passengers by an amazingly successful raid by Israel will have a tendency to deter any further attempts at hijacking aircraft or any attempts at blackmailing Israel to release prisoners serving jail sentences in that country. From now on these terrorists will know that their own lives will be threatened, not that of any hostages they may take.
If this country now attempts to create a situation where we have the least severe penalty of most western nations for hijackings, then the very opposite will be true. Rather than flying aircraft to Uganda, hijackers will have them flown to Canada, particularly if their country does not have an extradition agreement with Canada. The worst penalty they can get in Canada will be life imprisonment. Their lives will not be in jeopardy. We are taking what must be considered in the eyes of the world a very backward step in attempting to control the hijacking of aircraft. This is a modern problem that has only come into being in the last five or six years. We should wrestle with it, and we should enforce the law as it now stands. We should not try to amend it as the Solicitor General is attempting to do through this bill.
I wholeheartedly support the two amendments moved by hon. members, the one before me being the amendment by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta. It demands the attention of the House, and now has the attention of the whole country. The entire country is in complete support of the amendment put forward today. Members of parliament on all sides of the House would be doing the country a service in voting for the amendment whenever it comes to a vote, on Thursday night or at some other time.
It would not detract very much from the beliefs of abolitionists to vote in favour of retaining the death sentence for those who are convicted of the crime of hijacking where bodily harm occurs during the commission thereof. Surely that would not be asking too much of those who believe in abolition. This is an horrendous crime which is very difficult to stop. Many innocent people's lives are endangered through no fault of their own. Surely the minister, if he had the good of the country at heart, would accept this motion moved by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta.
There is one other thing that comes to my mind when dealing with this subject matter. This bill left the House and went to committee where the committee refused to hear any witnesses except the minister. Had we been able
July 6, 1976

to call witnesses of the CP or Air Canada Airlines to give evidence before the committee, and perhaps officials of some U.S. airlines who have experienced hijacking a number of times, we might have heard evidence from those people who are responsible for the operation of aircraft, and for that matter ships, who firmly believe that the death penalty should be retained in respect of any such act of piracy.
The government in haste, or in an attempt to cover the facts and keep the public ignorant of the true state, rammed this bill through committee in a shameful fashion. The subject matter of this measure has been around Canada for a very long time. The government should have been prepared to have its legislation stand the scrutiny a good committee would have given it, and I know that committee would have given it that scrutiny had it been able to call witnesses and hear evidence. This is one of those things I will never be able to understand.
The minister knows he is moving against the will of the people. One might have thought that by having witnesses appear before the committee the minister in essence might have educated the people into believing that he is actually ahead of rather than behind them. However, in this way I think he is taking a retrograde step. I urge hon. members on all sides of the House to support the amendment which would retain the death penalty for the crime of piracy involving bodily harm.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
I
shall not take too much of the time of the House this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, but I do want to outline, if I may, the sense of the first amendment. First of all may I say that the new Section 214 deals with that type of homocide which we now have in the Criminal Code as murder. Basically murder, under the amendment submitted by the minister, will be broken down into two new classifications, first degree murder, and second degree murder. Right off the bat, in the reclassification of this type of homocide, anything that is not first degree murder will be classified as second degree murder.
In the new amendments there are a total, if my arithmetic serves me right, of seven broad, general classifications of homicide that can be classified as first degree murder. First, homicide is first degree murder when it is planned and deliberate. Second, homicide is first degree murder when the murder takes place by hiring an assassin, and that cuts through the verbiage of subsection (3). Third, homicide is first degree murder when the victim is a police officer or constable acting in the course of his duties. When a warden, prison guard or some custodial officer of that type is murdered during the course of his duties, that is the fourth broad classification of first degree murder. The fifth classification relates to a killing which takes place during an offence which we call the hijacking of an aircraft. In other words where there is a hijacking of an aircraft and murder or attempted murder takes place, then that is also first degree murder. The sixth classification is where a murder or attempted murder takes place during the offence of kidnapping or forcible confinement. Finally, classification number seven under the amendments submitted by the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) is where a murder takes place during the commission of a sexual offence such as rape.

July 6, 1976
Capital Punishment
Those are the seven classifications of first degree murder under the new reclassification submitted to the House by the Solicitor General, for which I congratulate him. The sense, the meaning, or the object of my amendment is to add an eighth classification for first degree murder. The eighth classification is in respect of any person who commits murder who previously has been convicted of either first or second degree murder.
I must admit that I have been doing a fair amount of pressuring and lobbying during the last few days about this. I feel that if an honest and fair vote takes place on this amendment, which hon. members will note does not deal with capital punishment but deals solely and strictly with a murderer who commits murder a second time, there are enough members who have indicated to me, regardless of how they voted on second reading that they will vote for this amendment. I suggest to hon. members that this is one instance in which we should not get emotional. It has nothing to do with the capital punishment issue.
I must admit that when I originally submitted the amendment my purpose was to make sure that all first degree murderers would be liable to the penalty of capital punishment. However, the Chair ruled that amendment out of order. But we still have this classification number eight for first degree murder. I submit it for the attention of members of the House because I think it certainly is worthy of consideration. The purpose is to make sure that the person who has been convicted of murder and who murders a second time is subject to the full punishment relating to first degree murder.
One might say that this is a pretty petty thing, and ask how often it happens. One might ask how many murderers are there who have been convicted a second time. I agree there are not too many, but there are enough. So far as I have been able to ascertain there are at least six convicted murderers in Canada now, and there is at least one person charged with an offence who has not come to trial, who have been convicted of murder a second time in the period between 1961 and 1974.
One thing I appeal to members of this House to consider, no matter what their philosophy and belief in respect of capital punishment, is the present law of the jungle that exists in our federal institutions. I merely point out that of the six people who have been convicted of murder a second time four have been convicted of murdering a second time in prison. I suggest to members of the House in general that this is something to think about. Under our present law a person in prison who has had a reduced charge of murder, which under the new classification would be second degree murder, does not have too much to worry about if he murders or attempts to murder a guard in the prison, or even a policeman on duty during an escape attempt.
I suggest to hon. members that my amendment could very well prevent the killing of other prisoners or the killing of a prison guard. It has nothing to do with capital punishment. It has everything to do with the deterrent effect in prison on some of those hard-core prisoners who simply are unrehabilitatable at the present time. I suggest that this is a sensible, fair and equitable amendment. At the present time there simply is no deterrent in the new

amendments brought forward by the Solicitor General that would deter anyone from killing a second time. Under this amendment at least there would be a deterrent if the person has previously been convicted of second degree murder, because it means in effect that instead of having a 15-year sentence he will have added to that at least a further 25 year sentence.

So far as I am concerned this is a free vote situation and I am ready to recommend that we support this amendment to make second murders, whether they be first or second degree murders, considered as first degree murders and subject to tougher penalties under these provisions. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased, although we were supposed to debate these two motions together, to see the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) agree to the amendment of my colleague, and I suggest that we only asked for a recorded vote because it is a free vote in the House and we want to ensure that every member's name is on the record. My colleague's amendment is somewhat of a victory in that if we had not put up a fight in the House over the bill, this amendment would not have been possible. We would have done what the government wanted from the start. We would have rushed the votes through the House and the bill would have gone through not in its best form.
My reason for putting forward this amendment to delete clause 4 is that I feel the whole clause should be deleted. Although my colleague would vote for his motion at the start, he will vote for mine when it comes up to delete the whole clause because we think it would be better than the first motion to which the Solicitor General agreed.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party

speechtext: I might change my mind like you did.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
As a retentionist I do not see how he can do otherwise but support the amendment I am proposing because it deletes clause 4. As it stands, section 214 of the Code reads as follows:
(1)	murder is punishable by death or is punishable by imprisonment for life.
(2)	murder is punishable by death in respect of any person, where such person by his own act caused or assisted in causing the death of
(a)	a police officer, police constable, constable, sheriff, deputy sheriff, sheriff's officer or other person employed for the preservation and maintenance of the public peace, acting in the course of his duties, or
(b)	a warden, deputy warden, instructor, keeper, goaler, guard or other officer or permanent employee of a prison, acting in the course of his duties,
or counselled or procured another person to do any act causing or assisting in causing the death.
(3)	All murder other than murder punishable by death is punishable by imprisonment for life.
I suggest to any of the retentionists on the other side that clause 4 in the new bill totally eliminates this protection for police officers or prison guards. Although I stress that I am in favour of retention of capital punishment for all people guilty of first degree murder, I agree with the proposal that people guilty of second murders be considered guilty of first degree murder.
We have to deal with this bill part by part because it is a free vote in the House and each member has to vote according to his conscience. There may be some members of the House who do not want capital punishment for all first degree murders, but I know that there are some abolitionists who are prepared to support this amendment because they agree we should have capital punishment for

July 6, 1976
Capital Punishment
anybody who kills prison guards or policemen while in the course of their duties. I hope I will receive the support of the abolitionists who do not believe we should have total abolition.
The Solicitor General has had numerous letters and briefs from various groups across the country, from police forces and from penitentiary officials who are concerned that their lives will be in greater danger if this bill is passed. I have had letters from people who ask why we have capital punishment only for murderers of policemen and prison guards. I agree it should be for everybody convicted of first degree murder. This is a law which has not been carried out and, as a result, we have put some policemen and prison guards in great danger.
The government chose to ignore the statistics put out by the Department of the Solicitor General covering the period between 1961 and 1974, which is a period in which we have virtually had abolition, although the government has twice passed bills which called for capital punishment for the murderers of policemen and prison guards. I think anyone involved in crime knows that this has been an abolitionist country for a long time, and that is one of the reasons we have such a serious crime problem today.
Between 1961 and 1974 the statistics show that there were six convicted murderers charged with murder after their first conviction. All six were initially convicted of non capital murder and sentenced to life imprisonment. In four of these cases the offenders were charged with a second murder which was committed in prison. That in itself points out one of the problems we will have if we end up with people spending 25 years in jail. Granted, they would have a chance of getting out after 15 years, but many of them will not because of the types of crimes they will have committed.
I cannot see the gentlemen who killed the policemen in Moncton, the two gentlemen who viciously murdered the RCMP officer in Surrey, British Columbia, the man who killed the policeman in Delta in my riding-

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: And in St. Boniface.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
-or, as the whip for the Liberal party says, the man in St. Boniface, getting an opportunity of getting out after 15 years. There are many vicious types of murder, and the amendment put forward by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) was a good one. I supported it, members of my party and members of the Liberal party supported it. That amendment proposed that after 15 years serious offenders should go before a judge and jury, rather than just the Parole Board, to decide when they can get out. I find it hard to believe that a jury would allow these people out of jail. Juries would make sure that most of these people stay there. That means a real problem for the people who have to work in the penitentiaries because these offenders will have to be controlled.
If hon. members have been to a penitentiary like the B.C. penitentiary and talked to people like Bruce and Lucas, or even watched what they do-I do not think one needs to meet them to know what kind of people they are-they will realize the problem we will have in this country if we abolish capital punishment and do not protect our prison 
guards especially. I think they should be protected even more than policemen because they are stuck inside institutions with people who will have no other recourse but, if they get a chance to escape, to take it, and when they get outside the institutions, they will take hostages, and we will have situations like the one in Calgary. In that case an escapee took his own life, and I do not feel very sorry about that at all. He had a choice to make. He knew he could either kill some people there and probably still not get away with it because he was surrounded, or he could take his own life. He asked for drugs and took his own life so he would not have to go back to jail. That is the type of situation we will have, but not everyone will have the conscience of the fellow in Calgary who took his own life. Some of them may take a few people with them, and if this clause of the bill were deleted we would be much better off.
I do not like to read things in this debate, but there have been a number of briefs sent to the Solicitor General by various police associations across the country. I think some of them were better prepared than others, but I would like to put on the record the brief sent in by the Calgary Police Association because the Calgary police have had some direct experience with some of these people. This brief is a good cross section of all the briefs which were sent in by other police associations. The Calgary Police Association brief starts by saying:
We appreciate the complexity of dealing with the problem of increased violent crime, and we sincerely empathize with the government's attempts to come to grips with satisfactory solutions. We would, nevertheless, like to raise several questions with the proposed legislative changes as contained in the bill. Our view of the issue "capital punishment", as we are certain it is of the government spokesmen and people in general, is couched with concern for providing community security, while at the same time, doing so without posing serious or unjust punishment on those who behave criminally irresponsible.
Their next heading is "Is the Death Penalty a Deterrent?" The brief goes on:
The death penalty, say its opponents, is no deterrent.
How can this be?
It is not being used. In Canada, since December 11, 1962, there has been no death sentence carried out, and yet there have been hundreds of innocent lives taken by the hands of violent criminals. Each murder was followed by a fair and open trial and due consideration for the rights of the accused person. If the Salk vaccine were given the same kind of test, there surely would be no cure for the dread scourge of polio today. One thing for certain-the death penalty is a deterrent to the criminal who is executed. He will not murder again and since in excess of 70 percent of serious crimes are committed by repeaters, a second offender may possibly have been deterred.
Then they discuss the public debate on capital punishment as follows:
Once again the matter of the death penalty is a matter of national concern. There are many different opinions and views being bandied about on this important subject. The question confronting people everywhere is this-Is it ever morally right for the government to take the life of a human being for his flagrant disobedience to the law, ie.-for a crime involving him in a capital offense?
Let it be said at once that the reason that we have so many varied and diverse opinions, such an endless number of opposing views, so many arguments for and against capital punishment, so many pros and cons of debate-the reason, we say is there is little or no leadership being shown over the past twenty years in the punishment and treatment of the violent criminal.
In both Canada and the United States there are several forms of perverted thinking. One of these is in regard to sex and another is in
July 6, 1976

regard to the punishment and treatment of criminal offenders. There seems to be a mass mania to be lenient and loose in both these directions. Laws and judges and juries take sides with the criminal and continually disregard the criminal's victim.
In preparing this submission, we came upon the most illuminating paragraph from the American Bar Association, an association of lawyers speaking on behalf of all American judges at a meeting some fifty years ago. Here is that echo from former and better days: "When, for the gratification of their appetites, or the promotion of their interests, lawyers, bankers, politicians, social leaders, both men and women, disobey and scoff at all law, they are siding with the cause of anarchy and promoting mob violence, robbery and murder; they are sowing dragon's teeth; and they need not be surprised when they find no judicial or police authority can save our country or humanity from reaping the harvest."
Contrast this quotation from the American Bar Association with the amazing statements made by the former Attorney General, Ramsey Clark, U.S.A., when appearing before Congress in July, 1968-Mr. Clark urged Congress to repeal the death sentence for federal crimes. Mr. Clark assured Congress that crime would go away or greatly reduce when all men learned to love one another. Mr. Clark mentioned "love" several times during his discourse, but could not predict when this happy state would arrive, however, one step toward hastening it would be to abolish capital punishment he suggested.
But to eliminate capital punishment, strict, just, effective and quick punishment for those humans who show they want no part of love and understanding-is to lay helpless, the meek, the kind, the decent and the law abiding, to the brutal twisted acts of the criminal.
Let us for a moment, travel to the promised land, California, U.S.A., and the eve of the defeat of Governor Edmund "Pat" Brown at the hands of Ronald Reagan, December, 1966. Governor Brown carried out his last major act-he commuted the death sentence of 9 men to "life without parole". Their records would fill these pages.
Later, in the same day, he again changed their new status to "life with possibility of parole".
Should this proposed bill pass and become law, the same thing will happen in Canada in 1976 through virtue of Section 25(1) (2) (3) (4). Page 12 and 13 of Bill C-84.
There are presently a number of people who are awaiting the outcome of this discussion to know what their future holds. They were all tried in an open court with all of their rights protected and have been found guilty of murder punishable by death.
What then is their fate? Will cabinet again flaunt the spirit and intent of a law of Parliament, or will they engineer one large "coup" and make all elected members part of their conspiracy?
The Association then asks, "what kind of homicide should be punishable by death?" and goes on:
What then is the kind of homicide that should be punished by death? Someone has put it this way; murder is the direct result of the unlawful plan leading to the death of another innocent person; or when another person dies as the result of another attempting to fulfill his desires, such as stealing, rape and other sex crimes.
Under the heading "Capital Punishment as a Deterrent" the brief continues:
Let no one confuse or use a pile of unreliable statistics or insufficient figures and factors when attempts are made to prove that the punishment of crime has no deterring effect. Chief Justice Taft, former President of the United States, said:
"I think the abolition of capital punishment is a mistake. It is a
deterrent for crimes of bloody violence. I have on hand more testimonials from criminals who said-I would not risk the rope".
The next heading is "How Do we View the Proposed Bill?" and the brief states:
(a)	We are opposed to the abolition of capital punishment.
(b)	The taking of any innocent life should be punishable by death.
(c)	We endorse the description of first or second degree murder as outlined in Section 214(1) (2) (3) (4) (5), Pages 3 and 4 of the proposed bill.
Capital Punishment
(d)	We endorse the intention of improved staff training and increased safeguards for maximum security institutions.
(e)	We believe the proposed bill will place prison guards and other prisoners in danger, by allowing the offender to remain alive.
The brief concludes:
In searching for a suitable method of concluding this submission what better authority could be found than the Honourable Ernest C. Manning, former Premier of Alberta and now a member of the Senate: "In this respect it is evident in society today, a strange and indefensible inconsistency. Many of those who are the most vocal in demanding the abolition of the death penalty because they hold it is morally wrong to put a murderer to death, are frequently the same people who are the champions of abortion on demand. In other words, they argue that it is morally right to destroy the life of an unborn innocent child, but it is morally wrong to exact the death penalty in the case of a murderer who has deliberately taken the life of another human being".
Let's put the blame where it belongs-on the lawbreaker.
Respectfully submitted, Calgary Police Association
I must still comment about the fact that we did not hear witnesses at committee. This type of brief, which is one of hundreds that members of parliament have received comes from people who should have been before the committee to put their views forward so that the media and the people of the country would be aware of them. Briefs like this never reach the pages of the newspapers to show what the feelings of the people are who are in the front line.
Sometimes I think that the bureaucracy, the people who get involved in making the laws, do not know what is happening in the field. I do not think the Solicitor General has gone out and listened to the people under his control. Certainly the RCMP, people in the penitentiaries, and people in the security field, have a totally opposite view to his on this issue.
I should like to repeat a quotation I used in the debate on second reading. In a book he wrote the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated:
I found it unacceptable that others should claim to know better than I what was good for me.
If he thought that at one time in his life, now that a majority of the country is totally opposed to what he is trying to do, can he expect the country to believe in him? Now he is asking the Canadian people to accept what he thinks is right for the country and I do not think they will.
The tremendous amount of mail which has arrived in the last few days shows that people are disgusted that parliament would pass a bill to which the majority of Canadians are totally opposed. The government can take a stand on an issue where the country is split down the middle, but in a situation like this the government is opposing the views of the majority who want some form of capital punishment.
I am prepared to compromise, Mr. Speaker. In the last two or three votes taken in this House on this issue we brought in compromise law. People knew there was no way an abolition bill would pass the House so they compromised. I wonder why, when there is close to two years left in the life of the present law, the government saw fit to bring in this bill. Why did it not carry out the law it voted for which ensured the protection of prison guards and

July 6, 1976
Capital Punishment
policemen? That law has been in effect ever since the Prime Minister has been leader of this country and certainly since the Solicitor General has held that post, yet they have not upheld the law. A number of executions have been stayed for a long time. Instead of trying to rush this bill through the House now why not delay third reading of the bill until the fall and stay those executions to the end of the year? It bothers me that the government wants to rush this through. The fact that it accepted the amendment of my colleague today is an indication that it should not be rushed through the House.
Those of us who decided we would stay here and fight some of the clauses of this bill to try to bring members of the House closer to the ideas and feelings of the people of this nation, were right. The people of Canada are going to remember, even if we should lose, that some changes have been made to improve the bill a little bit. Perhaps we are optimistic in thinking we might get some other clauses of the bill changed and that there would be some form of capital punishment for crimes committed in this country.
The Solicitor General circulated a letter from the family of a policeman who had been killed which said that they did not believe in capital punishment. Some of the letters of this type that we received are pretty strongly worded. I have a letter here from a Barbara Irwin whose husband was murdered in 1972 in metropolitan Toronto. It is worth putting this letter on the record so that people who read Hansard will see it. Not too many people have an opportunity of seeing what the wives and families of policemen who were killed have to say about the situation. The letter, addressed to the Solicitor General of Canada, reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Allmand:
I would like to voice my opinion on capital punishment, being the widow of the late Detective Michael Irwin who was with Metro Toronto police department. My husband was slain in the line of duty with Detective Doug Sinclair on February 27, 1972.
I have discussed this subject with my family and can speak on behalf of myself and my family. We all feel capital punishment should be brought back-not only for policemen.
I would like to refresh people's memories on our traumatic experience. When my husband was slain, the man who took his life was also slain, so I feel our opinion as a family is not revengeful.
My late husband and myself raised our children to respect humanity and what belongs to them. If they do harm to someone or something then they should expect to be harmed in the same way.
I am sure if your wife or children were raped or murdered you would not question bringing back capital punishment.
The cost to the taxpayer to keep this man in jail is far more than they pay the murdered victim's family.
We have one of the finest police forces, but I feel we won't have this reputation if capital punishment is abolished.
Why should these men put their lives on the line, to have their family's taxes keep the murderers in jail for 15 or 25 years?
I do not understand how parliament can say it is not a deterrent.
I have raised my children to be good citizens and respect the law by setting a good example.
The government should set a good example by showing they have some gumption, by making the murderers pay the price with their lives. One rotten apple is destroyed before it destroys the whole bushel. It should be the same in society.
I trust my opinion will be as valued as Pauline Maitland's. I am also a widow of a slain policeman and my family and I reside in Canada.
Sincerely, Barbara Irwin
It is signed also by three of her children.
Mr. Speaker, I am not quite finished so may I call it six o'clock?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had used most of my allotted time before the supper break. I wish to say one or two more things in support of my reasons for wanting to delete clause 4 of the bill. Before supper I quoted a letter written by Mrs. Barbara Irwin whose husband was killed in Toronto in 1972. May I at this time put on record a letter which Kathy Flannery, daughter of the late detective Michael Irwin, sent to Syd Brown, president of the Metro Police Association. She said:
Dear Mr. Brown:
I for one am very much in favour of capital punishment. Being the mother of a new baby, I feel I have more worries now than ever. I would like a little reassurance that when my child grows up, she will not have to put up with such a permissive society.
My daughter will be raised to the best of my ability to honour and respect the law and if she should do anything to break the law, she will have to pay severely for it.
I would not like to think that by the time my child is old enough to go out alone, that people such as Kevin Willden are back on the streets.
Perhaps if Mr. Warren Allmand or Mr. Pierre Trudeau saw the decomposed body of little Lisa Kowalski and put themselves in the shoes of her family, they would change their minds. Why take the risk that this could happen again?
I think that letter reflects the feelings of many in Canada. The feelings of such letter writers, of people whose relatives or friends are actively involved in the police force or work as prison guards, might be somewhat stronger than those of average Canadians, although I doubt it. Judging from the mail which members of parliament get, and the result of the Gallup poll-a poll which some people like to ignore in election times but which always comes within a few percentage points of showing the actual feelings of Canadians-the majority of Canadians want some form of capital punishment retained in this country. I think the majority feel that prison guards especially, and policemen, deserve special treatment.
Surveys I have conducted in my riding show that most people are in favour of capital punishment. The great preponderance of people want capital punishment retained at least for the offence known in this bill as first degree murder. I hope some abolitionists in this House will agree with us, show their support by the way they vote on this motion and thereby retain capital punishment for the murderers of policemen and prison guards. I should like to see the penalty retained for all who commit first degree murder but am prepared to accept a compromise if the majority of the members of this House feel it is necessary.
I shall close by quoting what a United States judge said some years ago about deterrence:

July 6, 1976

The death penalty is a warning, just like a lighthouse throwing its beams out to sea. We hear about shipwrecks, but we do not hear about the ships that the lighthouse guides safely on their way. We do not have proof of the number of ships it saves, but we do not tear the lighthouse down.
Those words are appropriate to this bill. I hope we shall not tear our system down by abolishing capital punishment for the offences mentioned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words in support of amendment No. 13 to Bill C-84. This amendment modifies Bill C-84, an act to amend the Criminal Code, by eliminating clause 4, and I believe it is one of the most important amendments to be discussed today. Four amendments have already been passed by the House. We are now discussing the fifth of 29. This is encouraging, and in my opinion the House will be able to adjourn in a month.
I believe that motion No. 13 is the most important of the amendments since it concerns the safety of policemen and prison guards. I have already talked about this during the other debates that we have had on capital punishment, but today I have realized, Mr. Speaker, that there is a considerable difference between section 4 in its present form and what the minister wants us to adopt.
The amendment reads as follows:
214. (1) Murder is punishable by death or is punishable by imprisonment for life.
(2)	Murder is punishable by death, in respect of any person, where such person by his own act caused or assisted in causing the death of
(a)	a police officer, police constable, constable, sheriff, deputy sheriff, sheriff's officer or other person employed for the preservation and maintenance of the public peace, acting in the course of his duties, or
(b)	a warden, deputy warden, instructor, keeper, gaoler, guard or other officer or permanent employee of a prison, acting in the course of his duties,
or counselled or procured another person to do any act causing or assisting in causing the death.
(3)	All murder other than murder punishable by death is punishable by imprisonment for life.
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the amendment which had been suggested during the last discussion had been accepted by the then minister who was the present Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand). I wonder why, since Parliament had agreed to this amendment, today, without consulting anyone, since the government has refused completely to have witnesses appear before the standing committee of the House, we are presented with a new bill that I consider completely ridiculous.
First, they start by categorizing murders. So we would now have first and second degree murders, probably ending up with third, fourth and fifth degree murders. So murders are going to be classified.
I now read the proposal before us:
214. (1) Murder is first degree murder or second degree murder.
(2)	Murder is first degree murder when it is planned and deliberate.
(3)	Without limiting the generality of subsection (2), murder is planned and deliberate when it is committed pursuant to an arrangement under which money or anything of value passes or is intended to pass from one person to another, or is promised by one person to another, as consideration for that other's causing or assisting in causing
Capital Punishment
the death of anyone or counselling or procuring another person to do any act causing or assisting in causing that death.
And further down, under subclause 4, the existing statute is somewhat altered as follows:
(4)	Irrespective of whether a murder is planned and deliberate on the part of any person, murder is first degree murder when the victim is
(a)	a police officer, police constable, constable, sheriff, deputy sheriff, sheriff's officer or other person employed for the preservation and maintenance of the public peace, acting in the course of his duties;
(b)	a warden, deputy warden, instructor, keeper, gaoler, guard or other officer or a permanent employee of a prison, acting in the course of his duties; or
(c)	a person working in a prison with the permission of the prison authorities and acting in the course of his work therein.
And finally, in subclause 5, the minister deals with the matter of aircraft hijacking that should have been included of course in the first amendments to the statute, that is amendments introduced this afternoon concerning piracy. However, this subclause deals with hijacking, kidnapping and sexual offences. Mr. Speaker, I would like to limit myself this evening to the matter of subclause 4 dealing with the murder of peace officers, sheriffs and prison guards.
As always the minister was very careful to put aside any conclusion contained in the previous act, that is to say that he ends up with life imprisonment as punishment.
This afternoon, while we were discussing motion No. 12, we heard a speaker introduce the motion, which would add a clause saying that if a prisoner who committed murder escapes or commits another murder, he can be given more severe punishment. The Solicitor General jumped to his feet, of course, to support that proposal. I wonder what more severe punishment he has in mind, when he says in his bill that first degree murderers will be sentenced to life imprisonment. It seems to me that the punishment that is more severe than life imprisonment is the death penalty. But he does not go beyond that. Yet, this afternoon, he said to us: we will give him a more severe sentence; but what punishment is that? What does he mean by more severe? Now, the amendment is ridiculous, stark ridiculous! When someone has really been condemned, I take the words to the letter, when they say after all that the maximum penalty will be life imprisonment and he tries to have us believe that there will be a penalty more severe than that, but what kind of a penalty is it? Another life imprisonment? And if the criminal commits a third murder, it will probably be a third life imprisonment? It gets so funny Mr. Speaker, that it is ridiculous.
I simply declare that the whole population cannot admit such a bill in the present circumstances. I think the minister, as all the others, has certainly received reports from police officers and prison guards. He received letters of opposition as we have received reports in which we are given the same percentage of the number of police officers who are opposed to Bill C-84.
Mr. Speaker, I do not understand at all how the minister can interpret his bill. He declares he is here to adopt laws which will protect the public and he is going to let the murderers absolutely free after a few years, and as I said this morning, I do not believe in these 25-year and 10-year sentences, as I did not believe him when he assured the House, during the last few years, that he was going to execute those who would kill police officers or prison

This will probably refresh his memory or he might learn something if he has not read this report.
I have the feeling he does not read any of those. He is one-track minded and goes straight in the direction in which he looks and I even wonder if he looks where he goes. So I quote:
The Police Chiefs Association of Canada studies with great interest the debate concerning capital punishment and we want to assure everyone that we have the same respect for the views of both abolitionists and retentionists ...
Do you realize their impartiality? There is no racism in all this.
In the briefs we already presented on that subject, we have clearly stated our position in favour of capital punishment...
Hear, hear!
... and at this time a discussion of the pros and cons would only bore you.

However, we wish to mention that so far one speech mentions our recommendation to create a committee of people representing the executive, the legislative and the judiciary to study in depth the permanent banishing of an offender and some alternatives.
Mr. Speaker, when we refer to permanent banishment, I am not sure if the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) knows that it means. Permanent banishment means capital punishment, to use the right words.
The current alternative advocated in Bill C-84 is not the result of considerable thought and is nothing but a deceptive palliative aimed at making us accept the abolition of capital punishment. This statement is mostly based on the comments made by the hon. Warrent Allmand ...
-this has to be the Solicitor General-
... in an April 8 address before the John Howard Society when that question was put to him. He said that a 25-year imprisonment sentence was too harsh but that we should first eliminate capital punishment and then direct our efforts toward reducing that imprisonment term.
It has been his idea, his obsession for ten years. It is not something new, this has been his target for ten years ever since I have known him in the House.
Such a philosophy greatly worries us because even if the full period of imprisonment in Bill C-84 did apply, it implies a much more serious threat for our society and particularly for the guards of our institutions. In view of this philosophy ...
Some people call this a "whim".
... we submit that the minimum sentence of 25 years as proposed in Bill C-84 is a blatant misrepresentation, considering that for all practical purposes an individual would have the right to make an application for a reduction once he has served the first 15 years.

Even if we retain capital punishment, the traditional commutation would have the same effect.
Considering that as spokesmen for the police forces in Canada, we have a knowledge of criminals which is available to very few people outside our profession, we regard it as our duty to express our deepest concern to you, our M.P.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that you are about to interrupt me. I believe my 20 minutes have come to an end but all the same I shall finish reading my letter another time. Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak very briefly in this debate on behalf of policemen and prison guards in the context of this bill. I believe they deserve special consideration because of the special kind of work that they perform.
July 6, 1976

If capital punishment does not exist for the killing of a policeman or prison guard, the prisoner serving a life sentence who attempts to escape has no deterrent to restrain him from killing a policeman or a guard in the course of that escape. He knows the only penalty he will receive is a continuation of that life sentence. This is obviously no penalty at all. I believe the penalty for killing a policeman or a prison guard should be capital punishment because that is the only deterrent to committing murder during an attempted escape from prison. Therefore I intend to support this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I spoke on previous amendments, once yesterday and once today, and I make no secret of the fact that I am really not prepared to speak on this amendment in the way I would like, though I must take issue with the government's position in this bill as it affects the security of police officers, prison guards, and people who are in danger of falling victim to contract killing.
Just over a year ago, 13 months, there were 15 people held hostage in the penitentiary at New Westminster. I know that at least one of those hostages was a constituent of mine. He was held as a hostage, together with others, for several days by men who have no convictions and no compunction in respect of human life. Last February there was another hostage taken at this same penitentiary by two of the same prisoners. Another constituent of mine was held at knife point by the same people. I met that constituent just a few weeks ago and found he was still not working after having been released on sick leave since February.
It seems to me we owe something to the men and women across Canada who are willing to place their lives in jeopardy for the security of others. We owe them at least protection from those who have no sense of value for human life.
Not too far from where I live there was a contract killing a few years ago. The price of that contract was $200. That is the price some of these people place on human life. If that is the kind of society we are willing to protect through this legislation, we have become bankrupt. We must re-evaluate our position on this matter.
The people in this House who are protecting those who have absolutely no sense of value for human life will be guilty when prison guards and police officers become the victims of future murderers. I am in complete agreement with those officers who are sending letters to those who voted for the abolition of the death penalty. I am in complete agreement with their position, that those people who voted for the abolition of the death penalty for the killing of police officers and prison guards should be held responsible for the deaths of future policemen and prison guards who are murdered.

Mr. Speaker, I thank you for giving me the opportunity to speak on the amendment of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds). Let me bring to the attention of the government some of the problems it will have to face if this amendment is not accepted.
Prison guards and policemen in this country are very disappointed over what parliament did a few days ago. They are now reviewing their positions in terms of the kind of work they are doing. Contrary to the Anti-Inflation Board policies, there will be only one way in which these people will remain in their jobs, and that is if the government is to come up with enough money to keep them. Certainly money is not everything, but some of these people may remain at their jobs if they are sufficiently well paid. Perhaps even then some police departments across the country will be able to recruit new staff. If I were a young man graduating from school at this time in 1976 the last job I would want to look at, no matter what it paid, would be the job of a policeman or prison guard.
The law as it existed before the vote did in fact provide a deterrent. Notwithstanding that the government did not live up to its own law, many of those who might have committed murder thought they might be hanged. They thought "the government did not hang the last fellow but they might hang me."
If I were convicted of first degree murder and sentenced to prison for 25 years with little hope of parole, and if I happened to be somewhere around 20 years of age that would mean I would be 45 or 50 when I got out, the uppermost thing in my mind would be how to get away for six or seven days of freedom. Circumstances might arise during my incarceration in which I would only have to deal viciously with one or two prison guards. Perhaps I

July 6, 1976
Capital Punishment
could overcome them and obtain seven or eight days' freedom before I was caught again and returned to prison to continue serving the 25 years, or another 25 years for having committed another murder. That would only worsen the situation, because the minute I went back to that prison I would start thinking again of how to get out for another eight or ten days.
Let me say in all seriousness that I think it is terrible and disgraceful that the minister, who is so adamant and so vehement in his position that hanging must be abolished for all kinds of crime in this country, is not in this House to listen to some of the speakers on this side who have very serious and legitimate concerns. If we are really responsible parliamentarians I think it is our job to do all we can to ensure that the government at least sees a little sense in what it is doing.
We have the question, with regard to law in Canada, of whether or not we should be going as far as we are. Should we be as lenient as we are in terms of what is happening all around the world? I remember the day when the use of the lash was abolished. What is wrong with the lash in the view of any citizen who lives in accordance with the law? All I am saying is that we should use it for sexual offenders, for people who continually commit crimes against society. It is a deterrent as much as hanging is a deterrent in respect of the commission of a crime against a policeman or prison guard. I say in all seriousness the government once again should take a look at this before this matter comes to a vote.
