Mr. Speaker, throughout the debate on capital punishment I have felt constrained to make a contribution on each motion, not for the sake of getting my name in Hansard-any member can do that at any time-but with a very deep seated concern over the direction of this country and the direction or the path our government is taking in the face of overwhelming public opinion. My concerns are no less, indeed perhaps no greater, for the safety of police, prison guards, and all those associated with that particular group that helps maintain law and order in our society. I have no wish to give them a special category, but the criminal element has elected to give the police and prison guards a special category.
I recall recently after the result of the vote on second reading the response of two murderers in Oakalla prison in New Westminster who said, "Great stuff, a guard a day". That, Sir, is the attitude of the hardened criminal. That is the attitude of those individuals who have no hope for redemption, absolutely none; who have absolutely no concern for law and order and who place no value on human life except their own.
We had the example some 18 months ago on the lower mainland of those two murderers who said that their kick that night, their pleasure, distorted as it may be, was to go out and get a cop. Mr. Speaker, let it be on the record, for the continuing respect of the RCMP and the control they demonstrated at the time of the capture of these two murderers within a matter of an hour or two, that they did not shoot them on the spot having witnessed the murder of a brother officer. What fear have these men; what fear do 
these murderers have? Are they concerned about a sentence of 25 years in prison? Many of them have spent almost that much time in prison on a variety of other charges involving crimes against society.
The public cries out in frustration over the attitude of the government on the subject of abolition. I can readily accept the concerns of those who voted for abolition and the manner in which they have had to agonize over this issue, as well as the pressures to which they have been subjected by their constituents. I recognize and respect these concerns, but I cannot respect anyone in this House who would vote for abolition for the sake of appeasing the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).

Now on this particular amendment I find it necessary to say something because of my personal experiences and also because of the references of at least six members of the opposition concerning the situation.
I thought I had indicated in my earlier speeches my absolute respect for people holding the retentionist view and my honest presumption that they hold the retentionist view because they think it would improve the situation. I hold the abolitionist view for the same reason, and I would normally expect the same kind of respect. I will not indulge in any remarks that I feel offended sometimes- and this is only a human foible-when innuendoes are made, but I will get down to the point and let those hon. members who wish make the innuendoes do so. Let me get down to the point at hand.
Since this was part of the previous law, I had to deal with the fact that unexpectedly I would have to take a plane to Moncton and attend the funeral of the two policemen whom I knew so well. The two gentlemen had worked so hard with youth and were so well known in minor football circles that the police force itself each year purchased for them a ticket to the $100 a plate dinner where all the funds were raised for amateur sports in that area. I happened to have been the guest speaker at each one of those dinners and so was vitally involved in this work in the city of Moncton. I stood in the cathedral and heard the archbishop say to us "God help us not to do what it would be normal for us to want to do, but help us to do what you would have us do, and so save our souls". It was not easy when you knew the young boy who had been kidnapped. It was not easy when you knew his father, his mother, and the children of the policemen. It was not unusual for someone to send you the photograph of the little boy crying over the coffin and accuse you of not caring.
So this was a calculated decision. At the risk of not ever holding another seat in this House in my life I decided that those whom I consider my brothers-and being a Presbyterian I think I might see them again-would understand me. This is my reason for voting in this fashion.

This amendment brings the bill into focus with the existing law because capital punishment for the murder of police officers and prison guards is the only form of capital punishment we have at the moment. This amendment deals with that matter.
I think it is worth while to remind hon. members at this stage that the study in committee of this legislation was really not very worth while or illuminating to hon. members who participated in that committee. I spent some time one evening in that committee, and the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) said that he really did not know what would happen in our penal institutions if Bill C-84 passed. There was some talk of building new and special facilities to deal with criminals of the incorrigible type who are dangerous, but he could not satisfy the committee or hon. members of this House that the approach of the government is the right one.
The minister just said we would have to wait and see. Of course he believes that his approach is the right one, but this is too serious a matter to be running a laboratory type of experiment, and it distresses me greatly that the government, which less than three years ago said that it wanted another five year period of experimentation with a limited type of capital punishment, now feels that it is very important that all stages of this major piece of legislation must be dealt with before we adjourn for the summer. In my view that in itself is an interference with the free deliberation and conclusion to be arrived at by this Chamber on this legislation.
There happens to be a penal institution in my constituency at Drumheller which has been referred to on many occasions as Eldon's house, but it has also been referred to as the crown jewel of the penitentiary system of this country. I think the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) should be congratulated for forcing the government to build that institution against all the expert advice the government was receiving as to why it would not work. With this piece of legislation the government is acting on the same type of expert advice, and we will rue the day we listened to those elitists who think they know better than the majority of Canadians.
I have heard hon. members questioning the hon. member for Kootenay West about whether 80 per cent of Canadians want the retention of capital punishment. I suppose there is no absolute way of determining the matter, but several of us have conducted surveys over the last number of years, and the figures vary from in excess of 70 per cent to in excess of 80 per cent. I believe the Canadian Institute of Public Opinion has shown that the figure is well in excess of 70 per cent. But I do not think anyone can seriously argue that the overwhelming view of Canadians is that there should be some type of capital punishment.
We hear the Burke philosophy expressed, and abolitionists can agonize all they want and bleed all over the Chamber because they are using their judgment rather than that of their constituents. I do not accept that particular philosophy of Edmund Burke. I am sympathetic to a
July 6, 1976

great deal of his thinking, but that sympathy applies to other areas. I think the people who send us here to do several things on their behalf, and when we are discussing matters such as freight rates, banking legislation or economic questions, things ordinary citizens do not have the chance to become acquainted with, they will look to us for leadership and for our judgment. After all, members of parliament have more resources at their command to help them to come to the right conclusion. However, the question of capital punishment is in no way similar to those types of questions.
When I made my speech at second reading I said that surely this is the type of question which is most suitable for a referendum. The government says there will not be a referendum because it knows its view would be rejected by Canadians at large. That is the only reason the government will not hold a referendum. It knows it would not have its way, but it is so elitist in its approach and so convinced that it knows best that it will use all the tricks at its command to make sure its will prevails in this matter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion moved by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds) designed to delete clause 4 of Bill C-84 is, in my opinion, extremely important.
Section 214 of the Criminal Code which was in effect in Canada since the last review of the Criminal Code provided for different kinds of murders, and at the time the House of Commons abolished the death penalty for the murder of any citizen but clearly retained it for the murder of prison guards, policemen, sheriffs or sheriff's officers.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, Parliament then suggested it was essential to support the police forces in Canada at the legal and governmental levels through a legislation stipulating that the murder of a prison guard or a policeman would be punishable by death. That is from section 214(1), (2) and (3) of the Criminal Code went.
The Solicitor General now proposes to abolish capital punishment altogether and just sets two categories of murders: premeditated murder and unpremeditated murder. In any case, the penalty remains the same-life imprisonment.
Mr. Speaker, I am not in favour of a police society. I do not believe either in a society where some kind of parallel power is given either to the armed forces or the police or the military. I believe in democratic power but I dream of a society where the rights of everyone will be respected and everyone will recognize his obligations. We know as professors, family heads, mayors or members of a provincial or a federal legislature that we can pass all the statutes we want but there will always be people who either will

July 6, 1976
Capital Punishment
not know them or not understand them or who will voluntarily defy them. That is why any organized society sets for itself means, limits, structures within which it must develop. That is how a system was invented for street and road traffic-traffic lights. You stop on red, you go on green, you use caution and stop on yellow. That is an essential law. It is stupid in itself but essential to the security of the public driving down the many roads of Canada and across the world. Laws of this kind for an organized society are found everywhere. As I said, Mr. Speaker, we had Criminal Code provisions calling for the death penalty for the murder of people paid with our taxes to enforce those laws whose only purpose is the protection of society. Under the old Criminal Code which imposed the death penalty to those convicted of the murder of a policeman or a prison guard, 11 persons were convicted pursuant to section 214 of the Criminal Code, and therefore, liable to the death penalty, because they deliberately attacked and killed police officers or policemen or prison guards.
These people thus deliberately broke the law, and I am not the one to say so, but the courts, the judiciary which says that they broke a law passed by Parliament. We all know that these 11 persons were shown mercy by the federal cabinet under the influence, I suppose, of the Solicitor General, this man who is so soft with criminals. And that is how, Mr. Speaker, these 11 persons are now sent to prison for life, but with the possibility of parole. I would like to say outright that what colours this debate on capital punishment is the existence of the Parole Board.
We pass a law, then the court states that a convicted person will serve for a given time, but inevitably the National Parole Board intervenes in favour of the criminal concerned and releases him, and thus the law of Parliament is twisted and so is the will of the court.
Mr. Speaker, during the second reading debate, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) argued about clause 4 of the bill. In turn 1 would like to do just that. He said that those who will vote for retention of capital punishment should think twice since they would have on their conscience the death of eleven people. I cannot do that. This is not a literal quotation but roughly the portent of what the Prime Minister said.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
It is funny, Mr. Speaker, we are talking about criminals here but we forget the innocents who are the victims of these criminals. Who is going to compensate these families? Who is going to protect these families, Mr. Speaker? It is not important. They do not talk about it but say that the lives of criminals must be protected, and the Prime Minister said: "I wash my hands of it, I cannot do this action, I cannot act as a hangman, let those who want to act as hangmen do this."
Mr. Speaker, since when can a government pass the buck to Parliament, when a legislation providing for the application of capital punishment for the murder of policemen, prison guards or law enforcement officers had been passed with a majority of votes? Mr. Speaker, this is a very serious situation. We pay for the maintenance of police forces with our tax money at the municipal, provincial and federal levels.
Let us suppose that tomorrow morning somebody commits armed robbery in some shop and that the police are called. Their first duty, that for which they are paid, is to go to the scene of the crime as rapidly as possible, armed, because our money is used to provide weapons for policemen to protect either the lives or the public and private property of individuals. That is the reason for the existence of police forces. It is so true that the federal government is now investing over $100 million in the Olympic Games to ensure security in case of danger or threats. On the one hand, enormous amounts of money are spent, the army is called, all the sophisticated techniques available are used, and on the other hand, when the supposed criminals are caught, they are simply released or told: You are liable to life imprisonment, which means a 25-year imprisonment with possibility of parole after 15 years.
Mr. Speaker, why would a policemen, if we adopt clause 4 as proposed by the minister, why would he go out and risk his own life to defend property which is not his own, a life that is not his and buildings which do not belong to him? Why should the law enforcement agencies intervene in a violent demonstration when the statutes of our country do not defend or support police action in Canada? Why should we, as Canadians, finance municipal, provincial or federal law enforcement agencies to protect our lives and our property if our own laws do not support them? This is why I say that the motion of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds) is valuable in the sense that it aims at ensuring that the most important democratic institution of our country, Parliament, which is supposed to reflect Canadian opinion, can protect the police.
We do not want a police society, we do not want a violent society, we do not want a society where people take an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. We want a society where the rules of the game are known, a society where we try to educate people as much as possible about their rights and their duties, but where we respect the laws that we pass. We have come to a point in our country where the legislation of the labour world is defied, where injunctions are
July 6, 1976

defied, where the police forces are defied; we are facing a situation of virtual anarchy.
People are worried. I have asked the following questions in my constituency: Do you approve the fact that the cabinet is changing the death sentence to life imprisonment when the Canadian judicial system has condemned the criminal to the death penalty as provided by Criminal Code section 214? This is what my own constituents, those who have shown confidence in me and who have elected me to the House, have replied: yes, 409; no, 1,885; undecided, 9; no answer, 138. This is significant. These 1,885 citizens of Lotbiniere are not violent people, they are not people who demand violence for violence. They are people who are worried about their safety. They are people who want to live in peace in their own country. They are people who want the policemen that they pay with their taxes to be able to do their work with the respect and support of the governments.
Mr. Speaker, I have asked my fellow citizens: In the case of premeditated first degree murder, would you approve the death penalty? Here is the answer: yes, 2,058; no, 274; undecided, 14; no answer, 95. I would like to note that more than 37 per cent of my fellow citizens who have received this questionnaire have answered it when a 10 per cent reaction is generally considered excellent. I have therefore received more than 39 per cent of answers, which shows how the Canadian people are worried about this situation. What we deplore is the fact that the cabinet does not respect the legislation passed by Parliament.
When we adopted Criminal Code section 214, the minister-and I remember that debate, I was sitting in the gallery-said that we would apply the death penalty in the case of murders of police officers or prison guards. Let us go back to that context. The death penalty was never applied. The cabinet found a way to bypass the wishes of the members as expressed in the House.
The minister says today that those guilty of first degree murder will be sentenced to 25 years imprisonment, which he calls "life imprisonment," and that after a 15-year period they will be eligible for parole. Mr. Speaker, I don't believe him. I claim that the criminals will be set free before the end of the 15-year period. Why? For good behaviour. I have no reason to believe the word or the good will of the Solicitor General because, Mr. Speaker if I rely on past experience, I have been deluded. I cannot believe him. If somebody could assure me that the laws voted by Parliament and dealing with the application of justice in Canada would be respected, my judgement on the application of the death penalty would probably be different. But I have no choice. This is my sole resource as a member of Parliament as I showed you by expressing the opinion of my constituents. This is my sole resource to try, with others, to ensure a minimum of security in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, no one can laugh at people forever, no one can exploit their good faith and their ignorance forever. The Olympic Games will cost more than one billion and a few million dollars of our taxes. For the Olympic Games, we are going to invest in excess of $100 million of our taxes to ensure the protection of personalities, politicians and athletes. Why do we spend $100 million to ensure the protection if, in any case, whatever crime might be committed on these premises, either piracy, high treason or
Capital Punishment
deliberate murder, we will not move to condemn the criminals? Mr. Speaker, there is a limit, if we really want order in society. The government uses the police forces and the armed forces of our country to escort athletes along the Trans-Canada Highway. In Quebec for example, they are being installed in Granby and a number of other places around Bromont. This excites people and creates an illusion that this government truly wants to ensure protection. But in fact, what are we going to do with criminals we catch, if there are any, which is not to be hoped.

speechtext: Give them an Olympic medal!

speechtext:
They probably will get an Olympic medal, if the logic of the Solicitor General is to be followed. That is totally ridiculous. Our police forces need encouragement and if clause 4 of the bill is not amended, I fear that if this government refuses to implement it, police forces will do so in the field. That probably is what will happen. Police officers called on the scene of a hold-up or violent crime will implement capital punishment to save their own lives, knowing full well that this government does not take its responsibilities. Police forces will take their own responsibilities.
Somebody told me recently that police force regulations provide that one shot shall be fired in the air as a warning before a shot can be fired at the criminal. From now on, after the Solicitor General's bill has passed, it will be one shot at the criminal and then one shot in the air, to warn him he has been fired at. That is utterly ridiculous. Either we want an organized society or we don't.
It is time we come back to earth and face facts. Mr. Speaker, the other night before the House I was talking about the taking of hostages in a Montreal schoolbus. There were then some gun shots, you will remember, and at that time, Mr. Speaker, the police stepped in. What could we read in the newspapers following that? Some public servants castigated the police for stepping in too quickly.
Mr. Speaker, that shows us how far anarchy has progressed in this country. And I repeat what I was saying earlier: I do not want to live in a police society, but I just want to live in a society where people respect one another, but in a society which punishes, governs or arrests those who do not want to obey traffic regulations. Mr. Speaker, when driving down the streets we stop on red lights and go ahead on green ones-

Mr. Speaker, that is the highway code in our society. Then, what do we do when an hon. member, a minister, a citizen fails to comply with the rule of the road? What happens? We say that everyone is equal before the law and we levy a penalty against him. Let us look at the case of the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Joyal) who recently was allegedly treated in an offhand manner by the Ontario Provincial Police for a mere summons for a parking offence. Mr. Speaker, is it not a ridiculous situation? We are extremely strict with a representative of the people for a mere parking ticket when in the case of criminals, who kill the father or the mother of young children, we just put them in jail.
Recently in Granby we had the case of someone who was convicted of murder and sentenced, if I am correct, to six months imprisonment considering his social status, the fact that it was a first offence and so on. What example do we give to society? I do not say, Mr. Speaker, that we should be strict but I say that we should be fair.
If, as citizens and MPs, we can accept that an hon. member be treated offhandedly by a police force for a petty offence, should we not, Mr. Speaker, insist upon adequate measures, corresponding to the seriousness of the crime, in the case of murders where innocents loses their lives? Mr. Speaker, only then will our society be really treated equitably. That is important and I want to close on that, Mr. Speaker. I do not believe in the law of retaliation, nor do I believe in an eye for an eye or a tooth for a tooth, but I would like to see a society in which there are minimum standards to respect, in which everyone knows the rules of the game.
We have reached the point where we want to control the use of firearms by innocent people through Bill C-83, but this bill does not control that of the criminals covered by Bill C-84. In other words, we attack honest people to give freedom to criminals. There is a limit to laughing at people! If we are serious about investing so much of the taxpayers money in the Olympic Games or about protecting public safety against the FLQ during the October crisis, let us now apply penal sanctions against those who break the law; otherwise, we are wasting our time.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been and continues to be my position that crimes of premeditated murder and certain other acts of premeditated terrorism in some instances merit the death penalty. The amendment before us, though it does not go as far as some of us would like, does restore the status quo as it existed before this issue was brought back to the House of Commons. Why was it brought back? It was brought back because the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) and the government did not see fit to honour the existing law which was passed in this Chamber by a free vote. Had that law been honestly applied it would probably have made it unnecessary to raise this touchy issue at the present time.
As I say, this particular amendment would restore the former situation by deleting clause 4 and restoring section 214 of the Criminal Code. As my hon. friend from Prince
(Mr. Fortin.]
Edward-Hastings has stated, prison guards and others in a like position do deserve special consideration. When one looks at the situation which prevails across the country today, the violence in our prisons and the crime which is being committed outside those prisons, it becomes obvious that society has not reached the stage at which the death sentence can be abolished no matter how much one might wish it had. For one thing, we still do not have in this country an adequate system of rehabilitation or a workable system of parole.
One particular situation that troubles me very much concerns a person who, for example, commits murder, is sent to prison and murders again. This time it is a guard whose life is taken. What does society do with this sort of individual? Does one put this person in chains or allow that individual, who may be a psychopath or just a plain, vicious killer, to remain in an institution menacing the lives of guards and other inmates? What do you do with a person who has demonstrated the capacity to kill repeatedly? That is the question to which we should address ourselves this evening.
One thing that has been lost sight of in this debate is that under the present law very few people who commit murder even face the possibility of being executed. The vast majority of the people who take the life of another do so in some extenuating circumstances. However, for the person who deliberately commits some kind of crime which most people regard as particularly abhorrent or unspeakable, there is no adequate way to deal with him at the present time until a way is devised to provide proper rehabilitation or other remedial assistance.
Anyone who heard the speech made by the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. MacFarlane) this evening would do nothing less than applaud his sincerity. Unlike many speeches made with a great deal of emotion, the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain did not get carried away with exaggeration, make unfair comments, or cast reflections upon anybody else, and he deserves a great deal of credit for his excellent speech.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
In putting the case forward for myself as well as perhaps for others who feel with a great deal of sincerity that there are cases where the death penalty is merited, in doing away with the kind of violence, admittedly abhorrent, that is administered by the state, with the consent of the citizenry and under the sanction of the law, we may be trading one system for another which will bring about a vigilante type of violence, even a type of violence that is administered by police and prison guards for selfprotection. It seems to me that at least an equal amount of violence will replace that which the minister and the government are trying to prevent. Until our system of justice, including rehabilitation and parole, becomes more refined and realistic, I cannot justify in my mind the total abolition of capital punishment.
It is fair to say, without being unduly sarcastic, that the Solicitor General in the administration of his portfolio, and the government in the administration of the country's affairs, have not demonstrated that they have matters
July 6, 1976

under the kind of control that would justify the vast majority of the people of Canada having confidence that their rights will be preserved and their protection improved by removing the death penalty. On the contrary, I think a vast number of people in this country feel a sense of betrayal on the part of the government in failing to provide protection for them in general, and for policemen and prison guards in particular.
I agree with all those who say that members of parliament must reflect their own consciences. Nevertheless I think it is incumbent on the government to recognize that perhaps as high a percentage of Canadians as 80 per cent feel very uneasy about the removal of the death penalty. In taking this extraordinary step surely the government should be able to point to some sort of improvement in prison conditions and in the administration of justice that will replace the security that many people feel the death penalty represents. Otherwise this would not be such an issue and you would not have eight out of 10 Canadians writing in to protest the death penalty being taken away.
If hon. members support this motion they will surely be coming to grips with the basic proposition that, in allowing police and prison guards to risk their lives to protect the rights and properties of Canadians, police and prison guards ought to have, as I maintain all Canadians ought to have, some sort of specialized protection. Otherwise, as a previous speaker this evening pointed out, it will become increasingly difficult to find people of sufficient calibre and initiative to make a career out of a very important and demanding occupation.
I hope the Solicitor General and the government will take into account the fact that up to this point in time they have not been able to improve or refine the administration of justice, parole services, facilities to reform criminals, or indeed do anything except to put in place of the death penalty a system which in many ways is more repressive and which makes the cause of prisoners more hopeless than it is today. Not only is the government giving people who are prone to violence and have nothing to lose an opportunity to vent their frustration by committing further murders, but many people convicted of murder will be sent to prison for a long time in situations where, if they were judged under the present law, they would be provided with some hope of rehabilitating themselves and re-entering society. Altogether, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that this is a very good amendment that will basically improve a very bad piece of legislation.

Mr. Speaker, this is the first opportunity I have had to say a few words on these amendments at report stage, and I rise to support this amendment. During the committee hearings we asked the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) about the changes being made by Bill C-84. The bill divides murder into first degree murder and second degree murder, and the penalty for murder in the first degree is 25 years' imprisonment. The bill refers to planned and premeditated murder, the killing of peace officers, police constables, correctional officers, wardens, deputy wardens, instructors and so on, and uses the term "without prejudice to the foregoing generalities".
The point has been made that guards, wardens, and correctional officers are responsible for guarding convicted
Capital Punishment
murderers for 15 or 25 years. During the committee stage we asked the Solicitor General whether these people will be permitted to be released into society under any circumstances. The Solicitor General replied that on humanitarian grounds even these prisoners will be released, but with an escort. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, if any person, regardless of his age, who has been found guilty of first degree murder under the terms and conditions of this bill and has been given 25 years' imprisonment is released on humanitarian grounds or for some reason or other with an escort, what value is he going to place on the life of that escort? That is why this amendment is so important, particularly if these people are to be released with escorts on humanitarian grounds.
Let me give you a little history, and I am not digressing. It was only a few years ago that humanitarian grounds under Section 26 of the Penitentiaries Act meant very special grounds. For a number of years it was necessary to get an order of a judge of the high court, and the attorney general's consent in the province where a person was incarcerated, before that person could be released on humanitarian grounds to attend the funeral of a member of his family, for example. Now this decision is made by an administrator, perhaps an individual without any knowledge of jurisprudence or of the law. Perhaps he interprets Section 26 of the Penitentiaries Act to mean any kind of grounds, because certainly people are being released now for any reason. Apparently many things are humanitarian. Some of the grounds are, of course, very unusual.
Let me review with you for a few minutes that intamous Geoffroy case. This was a person who was found guilty of the planned, premeditated murder of his wife. After he had killed her he burned the bed in the bedroom.

subtopic: NATIONAL GALLERY-ACQUISITION OF ROOM PAINTED WITH MURALS AT KARSDALE, NOVA SCOTIA-REQUEST THAT IT REMAIN IN NOVA SCOTIA
NATIONAL GALLERY-ACQUISITION OF ROOM PAINTED WITH MURALS AT KARSDALE, NOVA SCOTIA-REQUEST THAT IT REMAIN IN NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the all-inspiring reason we are gathered together in such large numbers this late at night began about 130 years ago in a place called Karsdale on the shores of the Annapolis Basin in Nova Scotia. There, as legend or modern history would have it, a British sailor deserted his fleet and sought refuge in the home of a wealthy merchant. While being given haven he passed away the winter by painting a room with murals. This room, which exists today and is the subject matter of this question tonight, is 15 feet by 12 feet by 6 feet 11 inches high. It has two doorways, a fireplace, and three windows, two of which look out on the Annapolis Basin. I am just trying to have people feel as if they were sitting there in that particular room.
The paintings have now become the subject of some controversy in the province of Nova Scotia. Miss Gretchen Pierce, who is one of the journalists employed by the Halifax Chronicle Herald, has described it in part as follows:
He covered it with a gigantic mural with many different scenes depicting life in Great Britain and the rural life of the Indians, scenes from the Croscup's own life,...
That is a reference to the person who owned the home.
... their marriage, Croscup's wife and their firstborn ... The walls of the room portray ship launchings, a group of MicMac Indians in the woods, a hunting scene, Queen Victoria with the Royal Family, and both St. Paul's Cathedral and Somerset House in London.
It shows Trafalgar Square, but in the days before the Nelson monument was placed there. The artist whoever he was-and again it is only legend which says that it was a British sailor who deserted who apparently has not left his name on anything in that room-did his work by pencil and then applied oil paint afterward. A few years back I understand there were several such painted rooms found
July 6, 1976

in Nova Scotia and other parts of eastern Canada, but now apparently the nearest one may be that in Wilmington, Delaware, where a home contains several painted rooms.
The National Gallery has acquired this room from its present owners and proposes to restore and remove the same to Ottawa so that the nation may join in this particular heritage. I do not quarrel with or fault the intention of the National Gallery, and indeed as a Nova Scotian I have to be a little shame-faced in saying that the problem really did not become recognized until after the sale had gone through.
Now, can this be moved? I have spoken to one of the most respected artists in the province of Nova Scotia, Dr. Donald Cameron MacKay, formerly the principal of the Nova Scotia College of Art, who says yes. Technology makes it possible to take a room, even a plastered room such as that one, cut it up in segments and move it many thousands of miles so that it can be reassembled in some other place. So obviously the issue is not only of whether this rather unique artistic heritage would suffer if it were moved. Perhaps the point is that Nova Scotia would be losing something that, even late in the day when we come to this conclusion, we think we should try to keep there. I will suggest a solution in a moment, as I did the other day when I asked the hon. lady the question which brings us here this evening.
There is something called the Atlantic Conservation Institute. It is funded by the National Museums. It works in my part of the world out of Moncton. It could carry out the work of restoration. It was not asked to do so in this particular case. I understand the work is being carried out by the arts faculty of Queen's University. I wish them well in seeing that the work is restored to its original splendor. Tomorrow Mr. Jean Trudel, the curator of early Canadian art of the National Gallery of Ottawa, will be in Annapolis Royal and he will be meeting with the Friends of the Painted Room, which is the name of the society that is trying to retain this for Nova Scotia. I wish them all well in dealing with what perhaps has become a rather difficult problem.
May I finally present my own suggestion. I do not like to see a deal cancelled. It was entered into a good faith by the National Gallery of Canada and the people who own the house. The provincial government could have been involved in this early but decided not to do so for reasons of its own. So I am not asking that the deal be cancelled. Rather I would suggest to the hon. lady and the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) that the National Gallery perhaps use a little imagination and try to make the best of what I think is a pretty good bargain.
I suggest that it not move the thing too far. There is the Champlain Habitation at Annapolis Royal, a few miles away, and I am sure there is a room which could be found there in which this unique painted room could be reassembled after restoration. The Annapolis Royal Habitation which exists in the constituency of my friend, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State (Miss Campbell), receives up to 190,000 visitors a year. This would not be part of the Champlain tradition, but it would be part of a tradition-

speakeroldname: Miss Coline Campbell (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: NATIONAL GALLERY-ACQUISITION OF ROOM PAINTED WITH MURALS AT KARSDALE, NOVA SCOTIA-REQUEST THAT IT REMAIN IN NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member was correct when he stated that this Painted Room is of concern to me. I would not like to see this artifact lost, and until the National Gallery stepped in that is exactly what was happening, as had happened to other similar rooms in the province. At present the Friends of the Painted Room are attempting to find solutions to this and to see how it can be kept in Nova Scotia and, more particularly, in the locale where it was found. But anyone who has visited the room will see that there is a big job of restoration to be done.
However, let me give some of the history of this. The board of trustees of the National Museums of Canada approved the purchase of the Painted Room in December of 1975. This decision was based on the board's judgment that the preservation of the room could best be assured through its acquisition by the National Gallery and brought to Ottawa where it could be restored and kept up under the proper conditions needed to keep such an artifact.
Before its purchase the director of the National Gallery advised the Nova Scotia government of the gallery's interest. In particular, the National Gallery wished to determine that the provincial government would not regard an offer to the room's owners, and its subsequent removal, as a loss to the provincial heritage. The reply to the director of the National Gallery was that the government of Nova Scotia was of course concerned about the departure from Nova Scotia of this art as a result of the purchase. However, it was felt that unless the province supported the gallery's initiative, the art might be totally lost. They recognized that the removal of the paintings was a delicate and costly task which the province was not able to undertake.
The removal to Ottawa of the paintings has been the subject of representations to the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) from private persons and non-governmental organizations in Nova Scotia. As far as the National Museums Corporation was able to determine before the purchase by the National Gallery, no local initiatives had been taken or were contemplated at the provincial or any other level to purchase, restore, and preserve the room for the public.
It is the intention of the National Gallery to instal the paintings in a part of the gallery devoted to the arts of the Maritime provinces.
The Painted Room will contribute to the national collection, the development of which is a major responsibility of the National Gallery. This involves acquiring works of art and artifacts from the various regions of Canada and bringing them to the national capital. If this were not the case, the national collection would cease to represent the Canadian cultural heritage in its totality. Perhaps these paintings may be able to be displayed when they have been restored in the local regions. Perhaps other arrangements could be looked at, but at this time the cost of saving these paintings and restoring them has to be undertaken, and the National Gallery has become responsible for this.

July 6, 1976
Adjournment Debate
In carrying out this responsibility, the National Museums are sensitive to local concerns and are doing their utmost to ensure that these concerns are given fair consideration in all such purchases.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION-MEDICAL CHECKS ON VISITORS FROM THE TROPICS
IMMIGRATION-MEDICAL CHECKS ON VISITORS FROM THE TROPICS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to speak about immigration and the spread of tropical diseases. I know that a great deal has been done in these areas, but I still feel that what has been done is not adequate to deal with the problem. I have stated the necessity for more drastic action to control the problem. I have stated that it is estimated that 10,000 people or more in the city of Toronto live underground and share corners with others. They are frightened, they receive no services, and they pay no taxes.
Apparently the federal government does not realize that Toronto is a multicultural city. The other night I talked to a girl from the city of Montreal who is now working in Toronto representing a firm there. She told me that on the subway one night she heard five different languages spoken, and that 52 per cent of the children going into primary school cannot speak English.
The field of children's health care is also becoming more and more overloaded, and a wide range of subtropical diseases is appearing. These diseases are being brought to Canada not just by immigrants. Many of them passed the requirements of a health department months before their immigration, and I would like to ask the minister if our standard has been met or the standard of the country from which these immigrants come.
I think it is basically unfair to allow an immigrant to come to this country and months or years afterwards to find that he is suffering from a parasitic disease. That puts a stigma on him and his family which is unfair. Since he may have unknowingly spread the disease to his family or others, that has made the health care system very costly.
I hope I will be forgiven for bringing to the attention of the Department of National Health and Welfare that many of these cases are missed for months or years because the medical profession does not have the opportunity of diagnosing subtropical or tropical diseases. To illustrate my point, I had a professional patient who suffered ill health for months. He had been in the east, and finally, after going around the circle, I diagnosed his problem because one of my associate doctors picked up the same disease while in Asia.
The point I am making is that we must be as careful as possible in diagnosing any disease which may be a subtropical or tropical disease. Let me add that parasitical diseases are accepted far more as a national occurrence in some countries than we can tolerate here.
I also want to say to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras)-and I am grateful to see him here in his seat tonight to answer me-that the risk increases with the length of time a person remains in Canada. However, the minister so far has been unable to state-and I can readily understand that-how many of

those immigrants there are and how many of them stay longer than the average tourist. Surely here is a case in point. The minister says a year or more. How about three months or longer, with the net result of the spread of infection mounting with the passage of time?
The minister states he has very little to do with Canadians who have stayed in those countries for a long time. Some work there for industrial firms or otherwise, or perhaps even for the governments. Is there any good reason why a thorough medical examination, particularly with regard to tropical diseases, should not be required when they return to this country?
My final inquiry has to do with foreign students from tropical or subtropical countries. Are they or are they not covered by insurance prepaid at universities? I am advised that many of them become sick and are afraid to go to the hospital or to see a doctor because they think they are not covered. Are they examined for these diseases when they come to our universities? Are they covered by health care insurance?
I want to tell the ministers involved that I have dealt only with the Toronto area, but there is also Vancouver, Montreal, and Cambridge, which has more than 10,000 Portuguese among its population. These cases present an aspect of medicine which is new to this country, and preventive medicine should be practised to stop and control these infections. The minister must now assure us that preventive measures will be taken and adequate care will be provided.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subtopic: IMMIGRATION-MEDICAL CHECKS ON VISITORS FROM THE TROPICS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the comments of the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard). The other day he asked me for some statistical information, particularly relating to immigrants and Canadians returning from tropical countries. I am not trying to dodge that. I want to tell him that we do not maintain statistics on the number of visitors precisely by classification of tropical or subtropical countries. That information is available, though, and the hon. member could actually collate it himself.
International travel statistics are obtained from Statistics Canada. We certainly use this information. If the hon. member were to identify those countries that he considers to be tropical, by reference to the latest publication called "Travel Between Canada and Other Countries" he would be able to find the statistics he seeks.
The second part of the question he posed the other day and asked again tonight was regarding visitors who stay in Canada longer than on an ordinary visit. I could give him that information if he would provide me with a list of the countries in which he is particularly interested. My parliamentary secretary outlined the procedures and the change in procedures quite clearly in May this year. The information is all in Hansard so I shall not repeat it.
In regard to Canadians returning to this country, the Department of National Health and Welfare has primary responsibility and screens all persons subject to immigration jurisdiction who are referred to that department by us at the primary inspection area or wherever we come in contact with them. The health screening procedure includes stool testing for the detection of parasitic diseases
July 6, 1976

and it is carried out on people coming from countries where parasitic diseases are prevalent. If the hon. member wants more specific information I would refer him to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde).
I do not consider this matter lightly, Mr. Speaker. I am alerted not only from other sources of information but by the hon. member's repeated expressions of concern. I intend to dig a little more into this area than we have done so far although I think he should recognize that we have taken very specific action in the last several months, particularly with visitors who stay more than 90 days and people who may be employed in food handling, and also foreign students. We recognize the potential danger in these areas.
I will check Hansard for the more specific questions that the hon. member posed tonight and will get him complete answers at the earliest opportunity.

subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-POSSIBILITY OF INCREASE IN ALLOWABLE EARNINGS OF RECIPIENTS OF WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE
VETERANS AFFAIRS-POSSIBILITY OF INCREASE IN ALLOWABLE EARNINGS OF RECIPIENTS OF WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising tonight to address myself to the difficulty that veterans are having in attempting to live a decent life on the income they are receiving. While it is recognized that increases have been forthcoming under the War Veterans Allowance Act and the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act, there is an immediate need to review the amount of casual earnings and to increase it beyond the $1,000 for the single veteran and the $1,500 for the married recipient.
I realize that there have been periodic increases in the amount of casual earnings allowed but I am sure the minister recognizes that there is justification for a suitable increase immediately to allow veterans to cope with rising costs.
The government has recognized and has provided quarterly indexing to veteran recipients of the allowance, and if recognition exists in this regard it should follow that there should be a coincidental increase in casual earnings. However, since the need is immediate a simple order would put the increase into effect. May I suggest to the minister through the parliamentary secretary-and I know the minister always listens to my suggestions-that the increase be in the order of 50 per cent which would increase the earnings to $1,500 for the single recipient and $2,250 for the married recipient.
If I may refer to the act itself, it was implemented to recognize pre-aging of the veteran as a result of war service, and also because of need. The veteran recipient and his wife are now in their twilight years and in most cases the children of the family have gone on their own, having been brought up under difficulty because of the veteran parent being on a fixed income. I am sure it should be recognized that the veteran in this situation, or his wife who now might want to supplement their income, should be able to enjoy a bit of extra comfort, and the amounts presently existing restrict their ability to offer themselves for employment with any permanency. They often run into the embarrassing situation where overpayments are creat-
Adjournment Debate
ed because they might have innocently earned a little more than the allowable amount.
One of the most important needs that I see with respect to increasing the casual earnings of WVA recipients is that many live in their own homes which need repairs or improvements. Because of their fixed income they cannot afford to maintain them at a reasonable level; neither can they afford a home improvement loan under the National Housing Act or the costly material required, and until we can convince the government to expand the veterans' housing program to include a home rehabilitation item for veterans, an increase in the casual earnings would help the veterans to prevent the deterioration of their homes.
I think that the minister should also give consideration to treating as casual earnings the meagre amounts that a veteran might be receiving under workmen's compensation and the Canada Pension Plan, particularly for those who cannot work.
Under the War Veterans Allowance Act a single recipient receives at present, on an unmarried basis, the amount of $221.98, while the married receipient receives $378.48. For those who can earn, this would mean that the single veteran would receive $350 and the married veteran about $550, which he could earn with pride and dignity.
I hope that the parliamentary secretary, who is most sympathetic to the veterans' cause, will pass on to the minister my remarks so that I can receive confirmation with a positive reply as to the action the minister has taken, whether or not he has made an approach to cabinet and on what date we can expect an announcement for increasing casual earnings which are so direly needed by veterans under the War Veterans Allowance Act.
